sens: One who possesses exceptional physical or moral strength
One who exercises remarkable authority or power
One who is capable of producing significant effects
G2900.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes physical or moral strength: one who is powerful has remarkable vigor and capacity for action. In 1 Peter 5:6, it refers to the "mighty hand" of God, meaning His ability to act with strength, to lift up those who are humble.
2. It characterizes one who exercises effective power or authority: a powerful king, a powerful god, someone who can impose their will and dominate situations.
3. It describes what produces powerful effects, what acts effectively: a powerful word, a powerful action accomplish what they intend.
G2900.origine: The word comes from the root κράτος (kratos), which means "strength, power, authority." It is a classical poetic form of ancient Greek. In the Greek translation of the Old Testament, it primarily renders the Hebrew חָזַק (hazaq) and its variants, which express strength, robustness, the ability to hold firm. The same family produces other words in Greek such as κρατέω ("to hold firmly, possess").
G2900.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Peter 5:6. The Apostle Peter uses it to describe the hand of God: "the mighty hand of God." This expression describes God's ability and willingness to act effectively to lift up those who humble themselves. The image of the "hand" makes divine power close and active, capable of grasping and raising up. The context invites believers to submit to this divine power with confidence, knowing that it does not crush the humble but lifts them up.
G2900.portee: This word reminds us that God's power is not distant or abstract, but active and merciful. By humbling themselves under the "mighty hand of God," the believer acknowledges both God's superiority and His kindness: this power works to elevate them. It is an invitation to stop relying on one's own strength and to lean on God's strength.

sens: To become or make physically strong
To affirm spiritually
To make courageous or resolute
G2901.detail:
1. The word first describes physical growth and development of the body: John the Baptist and Jesus as children "grew strong" (Luke 1:80; Luke 2:40), meaning they gained strength and physical vigor.
2. It then applies to the inner and spiritual strengthening of a person: God strengthens the believer "in the inner man" by His Spirit (Ephesians 3:16), that is, at the deepest level of their soul and faith.
3. The word also expresses strengthening in confidence and resolution: Paul exhorts the Corinthians to "be strong" in faith, to stand firm in the face of trials (1 Corinthians 16:13), which requires a form of personal courage.
G2901.origine: The word comes from the root κράτος (kratos), which means "strength" or "power." It is a later form of the verb κρατύνω (kratynō), which carries the same meaning. In the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament, this verb often renders the Hebrew חָזַק (hazaq), which evokes solidity, firmness, and physical and moral resistance — the idea of something that holds firm and does not waver.
G2901.emploi: The verb κραταιόω appears 4 times in the New Testament, always in relation to vital strengthening. Two instances describe the natural growth of children: Jesus and John the Baptist grew strong during their childhood, combining physical development with inner maturity. Two others place strengthening in the spiritual realm: Paul asks the Corinthians to strengthen themselves in faith, while in Ephesians he prays that God strengthens believers by His Spirit. The passage in Ephesians 3:16 emphasizes that this strengthening is not a personal conquest, but a divine gift that penetrates to the "inner man."
G2901.portee: This word reminds the believer that strength is not a quality closed in on itself. In the child Jesus, it accompanies wisdom and grace. In the adult Christian life, to be strengthened means both to draw from God and to actively respond to His call. The prayer in Ephesians 3:16 shows that true inner strengthening is a gift from God, not an isolated human effort.

sens: To take or grab someone or something with force
To stop, capture someone to hold them prisoner
To hold firmly, keep in hand
To maintain, observe faithfully
To retain, prevent from escaping or manifesting
G2902.detail:
1. The most concrete sense: to take someone or something with the hand or arm. Jesus "seizes" the hand of the young girl to raise her up (Mark 5:41); the disciples seize Jesus' clothes upon meeting Him (Matthew 28:9). It is a physical, immediate, and energetic act.

2. To capture or stop someone with the intent to hold or punish them. Jesus' enemies seek to seize Him to have Him condemned (Mark 12:12, Matthew 26:48); the guards seize Paul to prevent him from speaking (Acts 3:11). The word here carries the idea of domination and constraint.

3. To hold or maintain something firmly, without letting go. In Revelation, Christ holds seven stars in His right hand (Revelation 2:1): the word expresses stable and assured mastery.

4. To keep, observe, or faithfully hold a doctrine, commandment, or tradition. The Pharisees "retain" the traditions of the elders (Mark 7:3-4); believers are urged to "hold fast" to their confession of faith (Hebrews 4:14). It is a resolute and constant adherence.

5. To retain, prevent, or stop an action or process. Jesus tells Peter that the gates of hell will not "retain" the Church (Matthew 16:18 implicit); winds are held back so they do not blow (Revelation 7:1). It is to exercise mastery to block or contain.
G2902.origine: The verb comes from the root "kratos" (κράτος), which means "power, strength, domination." Κρατέω thus evokes the idea of using one's strength to seize, dominate, or control something. In Hebrew from the Old Testament, this word primarily translates "hazaq" (חָזַק), which means "to be strong" or "to strengthen," and "ahaz" (אָחַז), "to seize, take." The family of the word encompasses the constant idea of power being exerted and control being taken.
G2902.emploi: The verb "krateō" appears 46 times in the New Testament, particularly in the Gospels and Revelation. It first denotes a physical act: Jesus seizes the sick by the hand to heal them (Matthew 9:25, Mark 1:31, Luke 8:54). It then describes the arrest of Jesus, John the Baptist, or Paul: authorities seize them to imprison or judge them (Matthew 26:48, Mark 6:17, Acts 3:11). The word extends to the abstract idea of holding, keeping, guarding: one "retains" a doctrine (Mark 7:8), a promise (Hebrews 6:18), the confession of faith (Hebrews 4:14). In Revelation, it takes on a cosmic and theological dimension: Christ "holds" the stars, retains the winds, "holds" His word faithfully in the face of threats.
G2902.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us of two major realities: first, that Jesus acts with authority and power to save and transform (He "seizes" the sick by the hand), demonstrating His benevolent dominion over all creation. Second, being a disciple requires "seizing" and "holding fast" to faith, to the word of God, and to the promises received, despite opposition. It is an invitation to conviction, perseverance, and trust in God's mastery.

sens: Who possesses the greatest strength, the greatest power
Who is the noblest, the most worthy of honor
Who deserves the greatest respect, used as a title of honor towards high-ranking individuals
G2903.detail:
1. The word originally designates one who possesses the greatest strength or power, as used in ancient Greek texts. This notion of physical superiority or domination naturally extends to one who excels in their qualities.

2. "Excellent" means one who is the noblest, the most worthy, the best of its kind. It is a superlative that places someone above all others by their merits or dignity. Luke uses it when addressing Theophilus (Luke 1:3), an important figure to whom he dedicates his account.

3. It is a title of respect and honor addressed to Roman governors and high-ranking individuals. Paul uses it when speaking to Felix and Festus (Acts 23:26; 24:3; 26:25) — it is the polite and courteous form of address towards an authority.
G2903.origine: The word comes from an ancient Greek root meaning "strong" or "powerful." The superlative "excellent" expresses the highest degree of this quality. It is an adjective used in ancient Greek to designate what surpasses everything else — the strongest, the noblest, the best. In official texts and court relations, it has become an honorific title addressed to magistrates and powerful figures.
G2903.emploi: The word appears only 4 times in the New Testament, always to qualify or address high-ranking individuals. Luke uses it once in greeting Theophilus, to whom he presents his Gospel (Luke 1:3). Paul uses it three times in his defenses before Roman authorities: he addresses Felix the governor (Acts 23:26 and 24:3) and Festus (Acts 26:25). It is a diplomatic and respectful term, a common usage in the administrative and judicial language of the time to address Roman magistrates. The context always shows that it is used towards those who hold political power or a prominent social position.
G2903.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible recognizes the excellence and merit of others, and teaches the respect due to those who bear responsibilities. Paul and Luke, in using this title, show courtesy and acknowledgment towards authority — not out of flattery, but as a simple justice. It is an example of how a Christian can address rulers with honor while remaining faithful to their faith.

sens: Physical strength, vigor of the body
Power, authority to act effectively
Supernatural capacity, act of divine power
Domination, empire (particularly of the devil)
Glory and majesty in doxologies
G2904.detail:
1. Power primarily designates a visible physical strength — that of an arm, a warrior, a body. This is why Luke describes God as having "displayed the power of his arm" (Luke 1:51): the image of concrete strength in action.
2. More broadly, it is an effective power, the capacity to accomplish what one intends. When Ephesians 1:19 speaks of "the immeasurable greatness of his power," it refers to the divine energy that shapes creation and accomplishes salvation.
3. In Hebrews 2:14, the devil possesses "the power of death" — it is the effective power to cause death, a formidable domination that he exercises.
4. Acts 19:20 states that "the word of the Lord grew in power" — the Word imposes itself as an active force that transforms lives.
5. In doxologies (Revelation 1:6, 1 Peter 5:11), power is no longer an act but an eternal glory attributed to God: "To him be glory forever and ever!"
G2904.origine: The Greek word κράτος comes from a root that evokes brute strength, mastery. In the Greek Old Testament, it primarily translates the Hebrew עֹז (oz), which literally means "strength, robustness." The Greek word appears mainly in the context of divine power: God is never without strength; he reigns with unshakable power. This root has produced words in French like "cratie" (in "democracy": the power of the people).
G2904.emploi: The word appears 12 times in the New Testament, concentrated in the Pauline epistles and Revelation, and particularly in hymns of praise. At the beginning of the Gospel of Luke (1:51), it designates God's liberating action towards Israel. In Paul (Ephesians 1:19, 6:10, Colossians 1:11), it describes the divine strength communicated to believers to live in victory. A remarkable usage in Hebrews 2:14: Jesus defeated the devil by destroying precisely his "power" — the power he exercised through death. Finally, power constantly returns in the final doxologies, where it becomes a praise addressed to the eternal God.
G2904.portee: For the Christian, the power of God is never abstract: it acts concretely to save, to strengthen, to overcome evil. Understanding that Jesus has "destroyed him who had the power of death" (Hebrews 2:14) gives the believer solid hope in the face of fear. Recognizing God's "glorious power" (Colossians 1:11) invites trust in him to persevere. The doxologies proclaim that this power belongs to God alone, eternally — an essential statement of faith.

sens: To make piercing and loud cries, either to be heard or under the effect of strong emotion.
To express a request, an accusation, or a protest in a loud and resolute voice.
To express collective joy or enthusiasm, especially in a crowd.
G2905.detail: 1. To cry means primarily to produce loud and piercing sounds with one's voice, in order to be heard from a distance or despite the surrounding noise. Jesus "cried with a loud voice" to wake Lazarus (John 11:43), as one must shout to dominate a crowd. 2. The word also designates the act of demanding or accusing with force and insistence. When the crowds cry "Crucify! Crucify!" before Pilate (John 19:6), they express their will with vigor and determination, undoubtedly also with intense emotional charge. 3. Finally, to cry can translate the collective expression of joy or admiration: the disciples cry "Hosanna!" at Jesus' arrival (John 12:13), thus manifesting their enthusiasm and support.
G2905.origine: The word κραυγάζω comes from the root κραυγή ("cry, shout"), which conveys the idea of a loud and often discordant voice. In Greek, it is very close to κράζω, which also means "to cry," but κραυγάζω emphasizes more the noise and intensity of the cry. The word evokes the cry of both animals and humans — the demons coming out of the possessed "cry" (Luke 4:41) — hence its somewhat raw and emotional character.
G2905.emploi: The verb κραυγάζω appears nine times in the New Testament, almost always in John and in Acts. It is used to describe the cries of crowds (the disciples during the entry into Jerusalem, John 12:13; the crowd demanding crucifixion, John 19:6, 19:12; Acts 22:23), cries of demons (Luke 4:41), or a loud call (Jesus calling Lazarus, John 11:43). It also appears in contrast: the Servant of the Lord announced in Matthew 12:19 will not cry, marking his gentleness and restraint. The usage in John particularly highlights the emotional and collective strength of reactions to the events of the ministry and Passion.
G2905.portee: This word reminds the reader of the power of the cry — one that expresses raw emotion, deep conviction, or collective protest. It shows how the voice of the people can unite for good (praise to Jesus) or for evil (the call to crucify him), and how Jesus himself uses his authority by crying out to revive a dead man. It is an invitation to discern what cry one lets out of their mouth and which one they join.

sens: A loud and sharp sound made by the voice
A loud exclamation, a collective call
A complaint or supplication expressed through cries
A confused noise of many voices crying together
An expression of pain or distress by the voice
G2906.detail:
1. A cry is primarily a loud sound emitted with the voice, distinct from ordinary speech: this is why it can be described as a strong and recognizable "voice," as when the woman who was to be the mother of John the Baptist "cried out with a loud voice" in praising Mary (Luke 1:42).
2. It is also a collective call, a loud exclamation where several voices join together: in the middle of the night, the servants raise a cry to announce the arrival of the bridegroom (Matthew 25:6).
3. The cry expresses a fervent supplication addressed to God: Jesus, in the days of his flesh, offered prayers "with loud cries and tears" to the one who could save him (Hebrews 5:7).
4. It is also the tumultuous noise of several people speaking at the same time: during Paul's trial, there was "a great clamor" where the Pharisees debated among themselves (Acts 23:9).
5. Finally, the cry can express pain: in the new world, God will wipe away every tear, and there will be no more "cry" or pain (Revelation 21:4).
G2906.origine: The Greek word κραυγή comes from a root that evokes loud and distinct noise, an unarticulated cry. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, it is used to translate several words expressing call, complaint, or tumult (צְוָחָה, שַׁוְעָה, תְּרוּעָה), showing that the Greek translators used it for all human cries, whether joyful, pleading, or desperate.
G2906.emploi: The word appears six times in the New Testament. It first denotes a cry of announcement (Matthew 25:6) or joyful exclamation (Luke 1:42). It then describes the tumult of crowds — the clamor of a passionate legal debate (Acts 23:9) — or the agitated cries that the believer must abandon (Ephesians 4:31, where clamor is added to bitterness and anger). It also has a profound spiritual dimension: the cries of Jesus to the Father express the sincerity of his prayer (Hebrews 5:7). Finally, it symbolizes suffering: in the world to come, the cry will disappear along with every tear and every pain (Revelation 21:4).
G2906.portee: This word reminds us that the cry is the voice of man laid bare before his emotions and needs — loud joy, urgent call, fervent supplication, or despair. By showing that Jesus himself prayed to God "with loud cries," the New Testament teaches that the emotional and physical intensity of the cry is not an obstacle to true prayer, but can be its most authentic expression. It is also an invitation: in a new life without pain, there will be no need to cry anymore.

sens: Flesh of an animal, as food
Carnal nourishment, as opposed to spiritual principles
G2907.detail:
1. Meat is primarily the flesh of an animal intended to be eaten. This is the simplest meaning of the word: it is what is placed on the table for nourishment. In Romans 14:21, Paul speaks of not eating meat, and in 1 Corinthians 8:13, he refers to meat as food that can be refused.
2. In these same passages, meat takes on a figurative meaning: it represents carnal food, a practice that nourishes the body rather than the soul. Eating or not eating meat thus becomes a spiritual issue — what scandalizes a brother in faith becomes more important than satisfying our carnal desires.
G2907.origine: The Greek word κρέας comes from an ancient root meaning "to tear" or "to slice," as one must cut the flesh to prepare it. It corresponds to the Hebrew word בָּשָׂר (basar), which means both "flesh" and "meat" and is regularly used in the Old Testament for offerings and meals. The same root can also designate the flesh of the human body, allowing the word to shift between concrete and figurative meanings.
G2907.emploi: The word κρέας appears twice in the New Testament, exclusively in Paul's letters in response to tensions in the Corinthian community. In 1 Corinthians 8 and Romans 14, Paul addresses the question of whether it is permissible to eat meat offered to idols or to observe certain dietary abstentions. These passages do not concern the food itself, but rather brotherly conscience: meat becomes a test of charity. Paul does not ask whether meat is good or bad — it is a neutral food — but whether the one who eats or does not eat risks causing a weaker brother to stumble spiritually. The meaning of the word remains concrete: it is indeed about carnal food.
G2907.portee: This word invites the Christian reader to go beyond debates about dietary rules to focus on what truly matters: love for one's neighbor and the preservation of his conscience. It reminds us that freedom in Christ is not absolute when it can hurt a brother. More broadly, it teaches that even material and legitimate things must be subordinated to charity. It is a lesson in voluntary renunciation: sometimes, spiritual maturity consists of setting aside what pleases us to honor those around us.

sens: Of greater value, of a higher rank or quality
More suitable, more advantageous or appropriate
Having greater moral or spiritual excellence
Surpassing in dignity or power
G2908.detail:
1. Of greater value, of a higher rank or quality: the word expresses a comparison between two things, one of which surpasses the other in quality or standing. When Hebrews 11:16 says that the patriarchs "desire a better one," meaning a heavenly city instead of an earthly one, we see the idea of a marked preference, a more desirable good.
2. More suitable, more advantageous or appropriate: the word can qualify what is simply more useful or timely. In 1 Corinthians 7:9, Paul writes, "it is better to marry than to burn" — this is a matter of practical wisdom: marriage is wiser for one who cannot control his passions.
3. Having greater moral or spiritual excellence: applied to eternal realities, the word emphasizes a profound superiority. Hebrews 8:6 affirms that Christ is the mediator of a "better" covenant established on "better" promises: not only a difference in degree but a transformation of the divine economy.
4. Surpassing in dignity or power: when the epistle to the Hebrews applies it to Christ or his priesthood, it marks that there is a hierarchy: Christ is better than the angels (Hebrews 1:4), and "the inferior is blessed by the superior" (Hebrews 7:7), expressing a relationship of dominance and blessing.
G2908.origine: The word comes from ancient Greek and literally means "stronger," derived from a root expressing strength and power. However, its use has broadened to designate what is "better" in a general sense, often associated with "good" rather than "strong." In the Greek translation of the Old Testament, it frequently translates the Hebrew meaning "good," showing how Greek has assimilated the idea of superiority to that of goodness.
G2908.emploi: The word appears 18 times in the New Testament, especially in the epistle to the Hebrews (13 occurrences), which uses it to compare Christ and his work to the old economy: his priesthood is better, his covenant better, his resurrection better than that of the patriarchs. In Paul's and Peter's epistles, it serves to compare two choices or two states of affairs: Paul contrasts marriage with the sin of passion (1 Corinthians 7:9), and he asserts that being with Christ is "far better" (Philippians 1:23). The word thus oscillates between two uses: practical comparison (what is wiser?) and cosmic comparison (what is more excellent in the divine order?).
G2908.portee: This word helps the believer understand that the Christian faith is not a matter of retreat or regret, but of access to something truly better. Hebrews uses it to show that Christ is incomparably superior to all that has preceded him: to believe in him is to cling to what is definitively excellent. For daily life, the word also invites wisdom: to discern what is better among good choices, not according to the world's criteria, but according to God's will.

sens: To fix something or someone in the air, attached from above
To be attached, held at a support point
To depend on, to rest upon
G2910.detail:
1. To suspend means to fix something or someone in the air by attaching it from above. This is the most direct meaning, as in Acts 28:4 where a snake remains "suspended" from Paul's hand. The word evokes the image of something hanging, held by a rope or a bond.
2. To be suspended describes the state of what is hanging, of that which remains thus attached. When Jesus is "hung on a tree" (Acts 5:30, 10:39), the verb emphasizes his body fixed to the cross, motionless and in pain.
3. To depend on, in a figurative sense, means to rest upon, to be founded on something. In Matthew 22:40, "the whole law and the prophets depend" on the two great commandments: like a load suspended from a beam, the entire Law hangs on and is upheld by them.
G2910.origine: The word comes from a Greek root meaning "to hang" or "to suspend." The form κρεμάω is a simple variant of the more common verb κρεμάννυμι found in ancient texts. In Hebrew, the verb תָּלָה (talah) expresses the action of suspending or hanging, and it is often what the Greek translates in biblical texts. The word always evokes the idea of something maintained in balance, held by a support point.
G2910.emploi: The verb κρεμάω appears 7 times in the New Testament. It first denotes the concrete action of suspending or hanging: a millstone around the neck (Matthew 18:6), a snake in the hand (Acts 28:4), Jesus on the cross (Acts 5:30, 10:39, Luke 23:39). More broadly, it is used for execution by hanging, a practice attested in the ancient world. In a figurative and theological sense, Matthew 22:40 uses it to express dependence: the entire Law "depends" on the two commandments of love, as if it were attached to them. Galatians 3:13 applies it to Christ "hung" on a tree, an image of humiliation and curse (Deuteronomy 21:23).
G2910.portee: This verb helps the reader to measure the physical and moral reality of the cross: Jesus did not just die; he was "hung" as a cursed one, according to the Law (Galatians 3:13), to deliver us. It also reminds us that the entire Law rests on the love of God and neighbor: nothing can detach from it, for all "depends" on it. The word reinforces the awareness that the Gospel does not abolish the Law but fulfills and establishes it.

sens: A very steep rocky or earthen slope descending to a lowland or body of water
Cliff or vertical side of a ravine
By extension: any place with a steep decline from which one can fall
G2911.detail:
1. A steep slope is a strong slope, almost vertical, that drops down — often towards water. In the three parallel accounts (Matthew 8:32, Mark 5:13, Luke 8:33), the herd of possessed pigs rushes down from the top of these steep slopes and falls into the sea or lake: the image is that of a cliff or a steep bank, inevitably deadly for the animals that throw themselves over.
2. The word also designates the geographical configuration itself: a steep and rocky slope, such as that overlooking the shore of a large body of water. In Palestine, such cliffs existed along the shore of the Sea of Galilee, and it is there that the event took place.
3. Figuratively, it is a dangerous place from which one risks falling — a biblical image of sudden downfall or disaster.
G2911.origine: The Greek word κρημνός comes from the verb κρεμάννυμι (kremánnymi, "to suspend"). The initial image is that of something hanging, overhanging — hence the idea of a vertical or very steep wall. In the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint), this word translates סֶלַע (séla, "rock"), emphasizing the rocky and steep aspect of the slope.
G2911.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament, all in the same account — that of the demoniac of Gadara and the possessed pigs — reported by Matthew, Mark, and Luke. The three evangelists identically describe the scene: the unclean spirits force the herd to rush down from the top of these steep slopes into the water. The context is dramatic: it is the site of the miracle, a real place overlooking the Sea of Galilee, where the abundance of pigs poses no problem (pagan region or decapolis). The word emphasizes both the topography of the place and the sudden, irresistible nature of the catastrophe.
G2911.portee: This word reminds the reader that the events reported in the Gospels are anchored in real and visible geography. It also highlights, in this account, the destructive power of sin and unclean spirits: they lead the possessed — and all that is near them — towards certain downfall. The steep slope is the very image of this irreversible disaster, which only the power of Christ can stop.

sens: Inhabitant of the island of Crete
Person from or native to Crete
G2912.detail: 1. A Cretan is an inhabitant or native of the island of Crete, located in the eastern Mediterranean. At Pentecost, Cretans were present in Jerusalem among the pilgrims from various regions and heard the good news in their own language (Acts 2:11).
G2912.origine: The Greek word "Krēs" simply designates an inhabitant of Crete (Κρήτη, Krētē). It is an ethnic and geographical relational adjective: it comes from the name of the island. In the Greek Old Testament, Crete appears as an important island, a land of navigation and trade.
G2912.emploi: The word appears three times in the New Testament. In Acts 2:11, Cretans are part of the Pentecost crowd who hear the wonders of God proclaimed. In Titus 1:12, Paul reports the judgment of a prophet from their own people regarding the Cretans, describing them as liars and undisciplined. In Titus 3:15, the context confirms that the epistle is addressed to the Church established in Crete. These usages show that the Cretans, like any human group, had a reputation and a characteristic (here, a tendency to lie) that Paul acknowledges with clarity.
G2912.portee: This mention of the Cretans reminds us that the Gospel reaches all peoples and cultures. It also shows how Paul, in directing Titus, recognizes the flaws of the populations he evangelizes with a benevolent realism: he does not hide the weaknesses of those he loves but works towards their transformation in Christ.

sens: Companion of the apostle Paul
G2913.detail: Crescens is a Christian who traveled with the apostle Paul. His name appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Timothy 4:10, where Paul mentions that he has gone to Galatia while he himself was likely in Rome in captivity.
G2913.origine: The name "Crescens" comes from Latin and literally means "the one who grows" or "the one who increases." It was a common name in the Roman Empire at the time, given to children with the hope that they would grow in strength and wisdom.
G2913.emploi: Crescens is mentioned only once in the New Testament, in 2 Timothy 4:10. Paul writes this letter to his young collaborator Timothy towards the end of his life while he is imprisoned. In this context, Paul lists several of his collaborators and their destinations: Demas has abandoned him, Titus has gone to Dalmatia, and Crescens has gone to Galatia. Although little information is given about him, his mention shows that he was a trustworthy worker in the service of the Gospel alongside Paul.

sens: Large Mediterranean island, south of Greece
A waypoint and maritime navigation site
Port and refuge for ships
Center of primitive Christian life
G2914.detail:
1. Crete is a large island in the Mediterranean, located south of present-day Greece. It appears in the account of Paul's journey to Rome when the ship sails past it due to difficult wind conditions (Acts 27:7, 27:13).
2. The island serves as an important landmark on the maritime route: sailors seek its ports for shelter. The port of Phoenix, on the island of Crete, was a strategic place where they hoped to spend the winter (Acts 27:12).
3. Crete is a place where the primitive Christian community was established. Paul leaves Titus there to organize the churches of the island, appointing elders in every city (Titus 1:5). This is why Paul writes his letter to Titus, which bears his name and addresses the organization of the Cretan churches.
G2914.origine: The name Crete (in Greek Krètē) refers to this major island in the eastern Mediterranean, well known in the ancient world. It gave its name to the Minoan civilization, one of the oldest in Europe. For the Greeks and Romans of the first century, Crete was a familiar element of Mediterranean geography.
G2914.emploi: Crete appears five times in the New Testament, all in the context of Paul's journey to Rome and his ministry. In Acts, it is mentioned four times in chapter 27: first as a maritime obstacle that the ship sails past with difficulty due to the wind (v. 7, 13), then as a potential port—Phoenix—where they would have liked to winter (v. 12), and finally as the starting point from which they should not have departed to avoid the storm (v. 21). In the letter to Titus (1:5), Crete is the place where Paul left his collaborator to complete the organization of the local churches, appointing elders and strengthening church life.
G2914.portee: Crete reminds us that the message of Christ spread not only in major centers like Rome or Jerusalem but also in peripheral regions. The island becomes a place where Paul entrusts Titus with pastoral responsibility, illustrating how the early Church organizes and structures regionally. The perilous journey recounted in Acts also shows how God guides His servant Paul through trials.

sens: Cereal cultivated for its grains
Grain used for human and animal food
Symbol of famine or high prices in Revelation
G2915.detail:
1. Barley is a cereal, a grain that the ancients widely cultivated in the Mediterranean world and the Middle East. It is a hardy plant that grew well even in less fertile soils than wheat.
2. It was used to feed humans and animals: it was made into bread, flour, and beer. In Revelation 6:6, barley is three times cheaper than wheat, indicating that it was considered a more common and lower-quality food.
3. In Revelation 6:6, barley appears in the vision of the riders of the Apocalypse, where it symbolizes rising prices and food shortages during times of distress: "three measures of barley for a denarius" indicates extreme food scarcity.
G2915.origine: The Greek word κριθή comes from the Hebrew שְׂעֹרָה (seʿōrāh), which refers to the same cereal. The Hebrew root evokes the idea of "shaving" or "cutting," in reference to the harvest. It is a common word in the Hebrew Bible, where barley is mentioned as one of the seven characteristic species of the promised land.
G2915.emploi: The word appears only once in biblical Greek, in Revelation 6:6, in the dramatic context of the revelation of the four horsemen. John hears a voice announcing the prices of wheat and barley during a future famine. Barley, less noble than wheat but more accessible, symbolizes here a survival food in times of great distress. Its price compared to wheat (three measures for one denarius) underscores the envisioned economy of scarcity.
G2915.portee: This mention reminds us that even in moments of eschatological crisis, God's providence remains: the horsemen have no power over the oil and the wine (announced immediately after), signs of life and blessing. The humble detail of barley, food for the poor, also speaks to the dignity that God grants to every creature and every food, inviting us to simple gratitude for our daily bread.

sens: Made of barley, this cereal with elongated grains
G2916.detail: 1. The word simply designates what is composed of barley, a common cereal in Palestine. In John 6:9, it is a young boy who brings "five barley loaves" to Jesus: barley was less prestigious than wheat, often consumed by the poor. In John 6:13, after the multiplication of the loaves, they gather "the pieces that remained from the five barley loaves," reminding us that it was ordinary bread, of the poor. The adjective paints a humble scene, where a child offers his meager meal.
G2916.origine: The Greek word comes from "krithé" (barley). In Hebrew, "seora" also refers to this cereal, widely cultivated in the ancient Middle East. Barley grows more easily than wheat in poor soils and dry regions, hence its association with simple and modest food.
G2916.emploi: The adjective "of barley" appears only twice in the New Testament, in the two verses of the miracle of the multiplication of the loaves (John 6:9 and 6:13). In this account, Jesus multiplies five small barley loaves to feed a crowd of five thousand men. The choice to specify that it is barley bread emphasizes the humility of the gift: it was not refined white bread made from wheat, but the food of ordinary and poor people.
G2916.portee: This seemingly trivial detail reminds us that Jesus takes the gift of the poor seriously. The child offers all he has, ordinary barley bread, and Jesus uses it for an incomparable miracle. It is a lesson of faith: what is small, humble, and ordinary in the hands of Christ becomes extraordinary and satisfies the multitudes.

sens: The decision rendered by a court or a judge on a case
A condemnation, a sentence pronounced against someone
The action of judging, resolving a dispute
The moral evaluation of conduct, the verdict on what is right or wrong
The judgment of God, His eternal sentence on the acts of men
A trial, a matter brought before justice
G2917.detail:
1. Judgment is primarily the decision that a judge renders after hearing both parties: it is the outcome of a judicial proceeding. In Matthew 7:2, Jesus speaks of the judgment by which you will be judged — the sentence you will receive.
2. Very often, the word specifically refers to a condemnation, an adverse sentence. Luke 23:40 speaks of one who "suffers the same condemnation" — he is found guilty. It is a judgment that falls upon someone as punishment.
3. Sometimes the word simply means the act of judging, the power to decide, to resolve a dispute. In 1 Corinthians 6:7, Paul speaks of a "trial" between Christian brothers — a matter that should be resolved internally, not before pagan courts.
4. The word also broadens to general moral evaluation: judgment concerns what is good or bad, just or unjust. Romans 2:2 speaks of the "judgment of God against those who commit such things," that is, His moral evaluation of their acts.
5. The judgment of God occupies a central place in the Bible: it is His final sentence on every creature. Hebrews 6:2 mentions the "eternal judgment," which determines the eternal fate of each person. Revelation 20:4 speaks of the right of judgment given to the elect.
6. Judgment can also be the present experience of receiving condemnation or punishment: in 1 Corinthians 11:34, Paul says that eating the Lord's bread unworthily brings judgment, a divine punishment.
G2917.origine: The word κρίμα comes from the verb κρίνω (krino), which means "to judge, to discern, to decide." The root refers to the idea of separating, setting apart — to judge is to distinguish the good from the bad, the innocent from the guilty. In Hebrew, this word often translates מִשְׁפָּט (mishpat), which means both "judgment" and "right" or "ordinance": it is the result of judgment, the sentence rendered. The entire family of the verb κρίνω (crisis, critique) revolves around this idea of discernment and decision.
G2917.emploi: The word appears 28 times in the New Testament, mostly in the epistles of Paul and in Revelation. It is used for the judgment of men (civil court or condemnation by others), but much more often for the judgment of God. Paul uses it notably to remind Christians that God judges actions, intentions, and even thoughts: in Romans 2:2-3, he asserts that the judgment of God is "according to truth." In 1 Corinthians 11:29-34, he speaks of the judgment received by those who abuse the Lord's Supper. In James 3:1, he warns that "teachers will be judged more strictly," suggesting that God's judgment weighs differently according to responsibilities. Revelation often uses this word for the final and inevitable judgment. Jesus in John 9:39 declares that He came for judgment — not to condemn definitively, but to reveal hearts.
G2917.portee: This word reminds the believer that God sees everything and that every act, every word, every intention will be weighed according to absolute justice. Jesus invites us not to judge others harshly (Matthew 7:2), for we will be judged by the same measure. For the Christian, judgment is not a vague threat: it is a solemn reality that should motivate integrity of life and the fear of God. But it is also a reason for confidence, for the final judgment passes through Christ, who knows and forgives the hearts that turn to Him.

sens: White or colored flower, cultivated or wild, symbol of purity and beauty
G2918.detail: 1. The lily is an elegant flower with delicate petals, found in the fields of Palestine. Jesus speaks of it in His teaching on trust in God: "Consider how the lilies of the field grow: they neither toil nor spin" (Matthew 6:28). He uses this flower to show that God provides for the beauty of creation without effort on its part, just as He will take care of those who seek Him.
G2918.origine: The Greek word κρίνον comes from an ancient root and generally translates the Hebrew שׁוּשַׁן (shoshane). This Hebrew name itself appears in several biblical contexts and refers to a flower renowned for its bright whiteness. The lily was a well-known flower in the Mediterranean and the Middle East, often associated with purity and nobility.
G2918.emploi: The word lily appears only twice in the New Testament, both in the words of Jesus recorded by Matthew and Luke. These two passages are parallel: Jesus invites His disciples to observe how the lilies grow in the fields without tiring or spinning, and yet Solomon, in all his glory and riches, was not dressed as beautifully as one of these lilies. The context is that of the Sermon on the Mount and the teaching on anxiety: Jesus encourages His listeners to stop worrying excessively about their food and clothing, for God takes care even of the flowers of the field.
G2918.portee: This passage reminds the Christian that God cares for the beauty and provision of the humblest beings in creation. If God clothes the lilies with such splendor without them having to exert any effort, will He not care for the believer who places his trust in Him? This image invites us to abandon anxiety and to live in faith, knowing that the Heavenly Father knows our needs and will provide according to His grace.

sens: Separate, choose, discern
Estimate, approve, have an opinion
Decide, resolve, determine
Litigate, enter into a lawsuit
Pronounce a judgment, condemn
Govern, exercise authority
G2919.detail:
1. To separate or choose between several things: the word primarily evokes the act of distinguishing, setting apart. This is the oldest and most concrete meaning, which is rarely found in the New Testament.

2. To estimate something, to have an opinion: to form a personal judgment about the value or quality of someone. In Romans 14:5, "Let each one be fully convinced in his own mind," this means having a personal judgment about what is appropriate.

3. To decide, to take a resolution or a side: this is to act based on a conviction. Paul "resolved" to pass by Ephesus (Acts 20:16), in other words, he made a decision, he set his plan.

4. To litigate, to enter into conflict before a court: this is to put one's case into the hands of a judge. Matthew 5:40 speaks of suing someone in court.

5. To pronounce a judgment, to decide someone's fate, and often to condemn: this is the most common meaning, especially when it concerns God. In John 8:16, Jesus says, "I judge," in the sense that his judgment is exercised over people. In Hebrews 13:4, God "will judge," meaning he will condemn the immoral.

6. To govern, to exercise authority over a people: in this sense, the word aligns with the biblical Greek that translates the Hebrew verb "to govern." In Matthew 19:28 and Luke 22:30, the apostles will sit on twelve thrones and "will judge" the twelve tribes, meaning they will govern them.
G2919.origine: The verb κρίνω comes from a root meaning "to separate," "to distinguish." In classical Greek, it primarily denotes the act of cutting, discerning, and then the action of judging in a formal sense. In the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament), it mainly translates the Hebrew verb שׁפט (shaphat), which means both "to judge" and "to govern." This connection shows that in biblical thought, to judge is not only a legal act but also an exercise of authority and governance.
G2919.emploi: The verb κρίνω appears 99 times in the New Testament. It is used in all the gospels, the Acts, and the Pauline epistles, as well as in Hebrews, James, and Revelation. Its meanings vary according to the context: in the synoptic gospels, Jesus warns against judging men by men (Matthew 7:1, Luke 6:37), while in the Gospel of John, the theme of judgment recurs constantly—both that the Father judges (John 5:22, 5:30) and that Jesus judges or does not judge (John 3:17-18, 8:15-16). In Paul, the verb mainly applies to the decision of conscience (Romans 14:3-5), to God's judgment on sins (Romans 2:16, 3:4), or to the resolution of personal will (1 Corinthians 2:2, 7:37). In Acts, it often designates the decision of the apostles or authorities (Acts 15:19, 16:4, 20:16). The word also applies to legal trials and the act of suing (Matthew 5:40, 1 Corinthians 6:1-6).
G2919.portee: For the Christian, this word reveals that judging is not a matter of passion or appearance, but requires true discernment—what Jesus asks when he says, "judge with righteous judgment" (John 7:24). It also reminds us of humility: we should not judge our brothers on matters of conscience (Romans 14:4), for it is God who judges. Finally, it shows that the Father has entrusted judgment to the Son (John 5:22), meaning that divine justice will be fulfilled in Jesus Christ. This word invites us to distinguish between our limited capacity to discern and the divine authority to judge.

sens: Action of judging, resolving a matter in court
Decision rendered by a court or a judge
Critical sentiment, assessment of a person or situation
Divine judgment, God's condemnation of evil
The final judgment, ultimate condemnation on the day of resurrection
Justice, just order, what is in accordance with the law
G2920.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the act of judging, separating the just from the unjust in a matter brought before a court. John 7:24 urges to "judge with righteous judgment," meaning to exercise this discernment correctly.

2. It is the verdict rendered by the judge: the decision that comes after examining the facts. John 5:30 states, "my judgment is just," referring to the sentence pronounced by Jesus.

3. The word extends to any critical judgment made about someone or something—a personal opinion, an evaluation. This can be a person's judgment about another.

4. The judgment of God is his condemnation of sin and evil. In John 3:19, the condemnation comes from the fact that light has come into the world, but men love darkness. John 16:8 states that the Spirit will convict the world "of judgment," meaning the reality of divine punishment.

5. The final judgment is the ultimate sentence pronounced by God at the end of times on all human beings. Matthew 12:36 speaks of the "day of judgment" when men will account for their idle words.

6. By extension, the word also denotes justice itself, the just and right order. Matthew 12:18 cites a prophecy: "I will put my name upon him, and he will establish justice among the Gentiles"—κρίσις signifies the establishment of law and righteousness.
G2920.origine: The word comes from the verb κρίνω (krínô), "to judge, to separate, to discern." The root evokes the idea of separating things to judge them correctly. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, κρίσις primarily translates מִשְׁפָּט (mishpat), which means both "judgment" and "justice," that is, the rendered right and the established order. This same root is found in words of the same Greek family: κριτής (krités), "judge," and κρίνω (krínô), "to judge."
G2920.emploi: The word appears 47 times in the New Testament. It is first used in a concrete and judicial sense: Matthew 5:21 mentions those who will appear before the tribunal to be judged; Acts 8:33 speaks of judgment without trial. But the dominant and specifically Christian usage concerns divine judgment: God's condemnation that already weighs upon the world (John 3:19, John 12:31), the examination of actions in 1 Timothy 5:24, and especially the final judgment, the last judgment that will take place at the resurrection (Hebrews 9:27, 2 Peter 2:9, Revelation 16:7). The word also designates the divine justice implemented: John 5:30 associates it with the justice of Jesus; 2 Thessalonians 1:5 speaks of God's "just judgment" towards those who suffer for the Gospel.
G2920.portee: This word reminds the reader that every act, every word will be weighed and judged—first by God now, then on the day of final judgment. This calls for moral and spiritual vigilance: to live justly, not out of fear, but because the presence and justice of God are real. It is also a promise: God will render perfect and impartial justice to each according to their works, without corruption or error.

sens: Chief of the synagogue in Corinth who converted to faith in Jesus
One of the first converts that Paul personally baptized in Corinth
G2921.detail: Crispus is a historical figure mentioned twice in the New Testament. He is the chief (the archisynagogue) of the Jewish synagogue in Corinth at the time when the apostle Paul is preaching there. His significance lies in his status: as the spiritual leader of the Jews in the city, his conversion to Christ is particularly noteworthy. Acts 18:8 reports that he believed in the Lord 'with all his household,' which means that not only did he turn to Jesus, but also his family, and they were baptized. Paul mentions Crispus again in 1 Corinthians 1:14, not without irony: he thanks God for having baptized very few converts himself (only Crispus and Gaius), to prevent the Corinthians from thinking that baptism creates a personal alliance with the one who administers it. Thus, Crispus represents a prominent convert and a man whose faith bore immediate fruit in his household.
G2921.origine: The name Crispus is a Latin name, common in the Roman Empire. He is a Gentile who, by embracing faith in Christ, changes his religious allegiance. His case illustrates the movement of the New Testament where many non-Jews and even Jewish religious leaders move from unbelief to trust in Jesus.
G2921.emploi: Crispus appears only twice, both related to Paul's apostolic work in Corinth. In Acts 18:8, he is presented as the synagogue leader who converts after hearing Paul preach. His status as a Jewish religious leader makes his conversion remarkable: he abandons his synagogue authority to submit to Christ. In 1 Corinthians 1:14, Paul cites him as one of the few Corinthians he personally baptized, alongside Gaius. This mention occurs in an exhortation against divisions in the local Church, where some claimed allegiance to those who baptized them. Crispus symbolizes a solid foundation of Corinthian faith.
G2921.portee: Crispus's conversion shows that no one is too attached to their status or position to accept the Gospel. A man who was a synagogue leader, thus respected and invested in the Jewish religious system, renounced his prestige to follow Jesus and bring his family along with him. His story encourages the reader to recognize that faith in Christ surpasses all human honor and that the grace of the Lord can transform even the hearts most rooted in another tradition. It also illustrates the impact of apostolic testimony: Paul's preaching bore visible and lasting fruit in Corinth.

sens: the place or instance where a matter is judged
the act of judging, the judgment rendered
the criterion or standard that allows for discernment and judgment
G2922.detail:
1. The tribunal is the place or official assembly where justice is rendered. In 1 Corinthians 6:2, Paul speaks of the 'judgment' rendered by the saints, that is, this divine instance of judgment; in James 2:6, it refers to earthly courts where someone is dragged to justice. This is the most concrete sense: a place, a court.
2. The judgment is the very act of judging, the verdict pronounced. In 1 Corinthians 6:4, when Paul speaks of 'disputes,' he refers to the litigated matters that Christians bring before pagan judges instead of resolving them among themselves: these matters call for a judgment.
3. A tribunal can also refer to the criterion or principle of judgment — what allows for the discernment of good from evil. This is the most abstract sense: a standard of evaluation.
G2922.origine: The word comes from the Greek 'kritès' (one who judges) and carries within it the image of judgment and discernment. In ancient Greek, we encounter compounds like 'sun-kritērion' (a joint judgment). Literally, it is what serves to 'krînein,' that is, to judge, decide, discern.
G2922.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament, all in Paul and James. In 1 Corinthians 6:2-4, Paul uses it regarding the eschatological judgment that the saints will render on the world, then regarding the arbitration of internal disputes within the Church. In James 2:6, it refers to civil courts where wealthy oppressors drag the poor. The three uses revolve around a rendered justice — whether divine or human, concerning a future judgment or a present instance.
G2922.portee: This word reminds the Christian that he is called to participate in eternal judgment and that he must live according to the standards of this judgment even now. It also invites him to resolve his disputes within the Church rather than before worldly judges — not out of fear, but out of faithfulness to his new identity.

sens: one who renders judgments and applies the law in a court
magistrate or civil governor
one who has authority to decide a legal matter
one whose conduct serves as a model or benchmark for judging others
God Himself as the eternal judge
Christ as the judge of the living and the dead
G2923.detail:
1. The most common sense is that of a person vested with judicial authority, tasked with rendering judgments and punishing or absolving: Jesus speaks of getting free from one's adversary before arriving at the judge who will deliver him to the officer (Luke 12:58).
2. In the Roman world, the word designates a magistrate or governor who oversees a province, like Festus, of whom Paul says 'you are judge of this nation' (Acts 24:10).
3. The word applies to one who has the power to decide a disputed question: the apostles refuse to judge material disputes, saying 'I am not judge of these matters' (Acts 18:15).
4. One whose behavior or words become a reference by which others are judged: the children of those who accuse Jesus will be his judges, meaning their own practice will demonstrate that Jesus is right (Matthew 12:27).
5. God is the ultimate and eternal judge: He will judge all things justly, and the believer stands before the Lord who judges (James 4:12, Hebrews 12:23).
6. Jesus Christ is appointed judge of all, living and dead, by God the Father to judge on the last day (Acts 10:42, 2 Timothy 4:8).
G2923.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb 'krino' which means 'to discern, separate, judge.' A judge is therefore one who separates the just from the unjust, who discerns and decides. In Hebrew, this word mainly translates the term 'shafat' which designated the leaders of Israel before the kings, those who governed and rendered justice to the people (like the judges in the book of Judges). The biblical context imbues this word with moral authority: a judge can only be impartial and wise if he fears God.
G2923.emploi: The word appears 18 times in the New Testament, especially in Luke and Paul. In the Gospels, it first designates the human magistrate before whom one is brought (Matthew 5:25, Luke 12:58). Then Jesus uses it to denounce the 'unjust judge' (Luke 18:6) who ultimately renders justice, or to remind that some will be 'your judges' (Matthew 12:27). In Paul, it refers to the Roman magistrate like Felix or Festus (Acts 24:10). But the word is mainly used for God and Christ: God alone is the true judge (James 4:12), Jesus has been given the mission to judge (Acts 10:42), and He will return as judge (2 Timothy 4:8, James 5:9). The epistles of James and Hebrews emphasize that only the Lord can judge justly.
G2923.portee: This word reminds the Christian that ultimate judgment belongs only to God and Christ, not to himself. It warns against the spirit of hasty judgment: beware of the unjust judge within you. It also assures that the believer will one day be judged by the just Judge, which should encourage holiness. Finally, it exhorts to seek reconciliation before arriving at the tribunal.

sens: Who has the power to judge, evaluate, distinguish
Who penetrates the thoughts and intentions of the heart
G2924.detail:
1. The word describes something or someone who possesses the ability to judge with finesse, to discern, to make a distinction between things. It is the aptitude to see clearly, to evaluate accurately. In Hebrews 4:12, the word of God "judges the thoughts and intentions of the heart": it does not merely strike at the surface, it untangles hidden intentions and exposes the truth of the most secret thoughts.
2. This power of discernment goes as far as penetrating the invisible interior of man. The word of God is not deceived by appearances: it sees beyond the lies we tell ourselves, beyond the motives we hide even from ourselves. It is a discernment that reaches the depths.
G2924.origine: The word comes from the verb κρίνω (krinô), which means "to judge, to discern, to separate." The root evokes the idea of sorting, distinguishing two things to make a judgment. In Hebrew, it is often the verb שׁפט (shaphat), which also means "to judge" in the sense of discerning and evaluating. The suffix -ικός (-ikos) forms an adjective that indicates a quality or ability: kritikos thus describes one who is capable of critiquing in the noble sense of the term, that is, to judge with discernment.
G2924.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 4:12. It designates the word of God as having a penetrating judgment faculty. Unlike modern French where "critique" often has a negative connotation (to reproach, to blame), the Greek kritikos here emphasizes a positive capacity: that of discerning well, separating the true from the false, good intentions from bad. In this context, the divine word "judges" (critiques) the thoughts and feelings of the heart, which means it exposes, evaluates, reveals them for what they truly are.
G2924.portee: For the believer, this verse reminds us that the word of God is not an inert word that can be manipulated or circumvented. It has a dynamic power of revelation: it sees through our defenses, it brings to light what we prefer to keep hidden. It is both an invitation to honesty before God and an assurance that nothing can escape Him. The Bible is not a manual to be consulted according to our whims; it is a living word that judges and transforms us.

sens: Knocking on a door with the hand or an object to request it to be opened
Figuratively, making a pressing request, insisting with someone
Seeking access to a place or a group
Knocking at the door of the heart, inviting to welcome
G2925.detail:
1. The primary meaning is very concrete: physically knocking on a door for someone to come and open it. It is the gesture made when arriving at someone's house and wanting to enter (Acts 12:13, where a servant comes to listen at the door). Peter knocks at the closed door where the assembly of believers was gathered.
2. This gesture becomes the image of an insistent request, a call that cannot be ignored. Jesus teaches: "Knock, and it will be opened to you" (Matthew 7:7) — it is an invitation to ask God with persistence and confidence, as one knocks until being heard.
3. Knocking at the door can also mean presenting oneself, seeking access or admission to a group or moment: the master knocks at the door of the house where he returns (Luke 12:36), waiting for someone to open for him. It is arriving and being recognized.
4. In Revelation 3:20, Jesus says: "I stand at the door and knock" — a powerful image of Jesus soliciting entry into the believer's heart, inviting to communion and personal relationship with Him.
G2925.origine: The Greek verb κρούω comes from a root expressing the idea of striking, knocking. It is a very vivid word: it first describes the noise and physical gesture, then enriches to express any request or insistent solicitation. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, the verb דָּפַק (dafaq) carries the same meaning of knocking at a door (Song of Solomon 5:2). The familiar word is κόπτω (koptō), which also means to strike, but κρούω stands out for the specific gesture of knocking at a door.
G2925.emploi: This verb appears 9 times in the New Testament, mostly in Luke. Most usages concern prayer or requests to God. Jesus repeats the call three times: "Knock, and it will be opened to you" (Matthew 7:7-8, Luke 11:9-10), equating the act of knocking with asking and seeking — we knock because we need to be let in, and God will respond. In Acts 12:13 and 12:16, it is literally Peter who knocks at the door of the house where the disciples are praying. In Luke 13:25, the returning master shuts the door, and those outside begin to knock, demanding to enter, but it is too late. In Revelation 3:20, Jesus knocks at the door of the lukewarm believer's heart. The word draws all its strength from this image: to knock is to be outside, to urgently ask, to be waiting for a response.
G2925.portee: This word reminds the believer that God listens to those who ask with perseverance: knocking is not a passive attitude, it is affirming a need and trusting that one will be heard. It also invites vigilance: being attentive to the knock that Jesus makes at our door, to His call for an intimate relationship with Him. It is a verb of active hope and openness of heart.

sens: Underground or hidden place where things are stored
A secluded place, out of sight
G2926.detail:
1. A hiding place is an enclosed location, generally underground or concealed, where one can store objects to protect or hide them. In Luke 11:33, Jesus speaks of one who "lights a lamp to put it in a hidden place": he evokes what would be absurd and counterproductive — to confine light in a hiding place instead of placing it prominently on a lampstand.
2. More broadly, a hiding place is any secluded spot, away from view, where something might be concealed. Jesus' image emphasizes that light is not meant to remain hidden; it must shine and be visible to all.
G2926.origine: The Greek word κρύπτη (kruptē) comes from the root κρύπτ-, which means "to hide" or "to conceal from sight." This same root is found in other biblical words like "crypt" (hidden, underground place) or the verb κρύπτω ("to hide"). The word literally evokes a hollow, a cavity — often underground — where something is concealed.
G2926.emploi: This word appears only once in the preserved Greek New Testament, solely in Luke 11:33. Jesus uses it in His teaching about the light of the Gospel: a lamp should not be placed in a hiding place, but elevated, to illuminate the whole house. The usage is concrete — the word indeed designates a cellar, a basement, a closed place — but its meaning is immediately figurative in Jesus' mouth: it is the Word, the truth that should never be hidden or silenced.
G2926.portee: This word from Jesus challenges the believer: the received Word, the truth of the Gospel, the gifts we have received from God, must never remain hidden or kept secret. Just as a lamp is of no use when confined in a hiding place, the Christian faith must shine publicly and inspire others. It is a call to clarity and testimony, and a warning against fear or shame in confessing one's attachment to Jesus.

sens: That which is concealed, invisible, out of sight
That which is done without witnesses, away from the public eye
That which is secret, kept to oneself, internal
What is deliberately hidden, the most secret thoughts and intentions
G2927.detail:
1. A secret in the literal sense: something invisible or concealed that cannot be seen. Jesus says that "nothing is hidden that will not be revealed" (Matthew 10:26) — he speaks of hidden realities that will one day be brought to light.
2. An action performed in secret, away from observation: giving alms "in secret" means giving without anyone seeing, between you and God alone (Matthew 6:4).
3. What is internal, hidden in the heart: the true identity of a Jew is not visible outwardly; it is what is "inwardly" (Romans 2:29) — it is the deep being, the soul.
4. The secret thoughts and intentions that are not revealed: the "secrets of hearts" (1 Corinthians 14:25), what no one knows except God. It is what truly happens in a person's mind and heart.
G2927.origine: The word comes from the verb "to hide" (κρύπτω). It is formed as an adjective describing what is in a hidden state. In the Old Testament, it translates the Hebrew "hidden" (מִסְתָּר) which evokes the idea of having withdrawn, being set apart. It is a word that paints the image of something removed from sight, inaccessible to ordinary observation.
G2927.emploi: The word appears about fifteen times in the New Testament, especially in Matthew and Luke. It primarily designates hidden realities that will be revealed on the day of judgment: nothing will remain truly secret (Matthew 10:26, Luke 8:17, 12:2, 1 Corinthians 4:5). It also describes actions or intentions that are deliberately concealed: Jesus refuses to act in secret (John 7:4, 18:20), while the disciples are to pray and give in secret (Matthew 6:4, 6). Finally, it characterizes what is internal and spiritual: true circumcision is that of the heart, "inward" (Romans 2:29), and the treasure of the soul is its "hidden inner adornment" (1 Peter 3:4).
G2927.portee: This word speaks to the heart of the believer by reminding them that nothing escapes God. On one hand, it invites them to renounce vanity — doing good without public witnesses (Matthew 6:4, 6) — because God sees in secret. On the other hand, it warns them that their most hidden thoughts will one day be revealed; it is better to cultivate the righteousness of the heart. This word teaches that what truly matters is what happens "internally," in direct relationship with God, away from human judgment.

sens: To place something out of sight, to conceal it physically
To remove someone from view, to put them in safety
To keep secret, not to reveal
To keep hidden, to make invisible or imperceptible
To remain hidden, to evade observation
G2928.detail:
1. To hide primarily means to place something out of reach of sight: the servant buries his master's money to conceal it (Matthew 25:18), or a city situated on a mountain cannot remain hidden as long as it shines before all (Matthew 5:14). It is to mask, bury, keep safe.
2. It is also to withdraw oneself from the sight of others to escape danger: Jesus hides in the temple to flee those who want to stone him (John 8:59), just as the disciples hid for fear of the Jews (John 19:38).
3. In a figurative sense, the word designates what is not revealed, what is kept to oneself: Joseph acts in secret, hiding his faith for fear (John 19:38), or a hidden word is a word whose true meaning is unknown (Luke 18:34).
4. To hide can also mean to render imperceptible or veiled: God hides his wisdom from the wise and learned (Matthew 11:25), and the Father hides the things of the kingdom in parables (Matthew 13:35).
5. In the passive voice, it means to remain hidden, to stay invisible or secret: the believer's life is hidden in God with Christ (Colossians 3:3), and he who has an ear hears what is hidden (Revelation 2:17).
G2928.origine: This Greek verb comes from an ancient root evoking the idea of sinking, digging, or hollowing out. It relates to the Hebrew verbs in the Old Testament translated in the ancient Greek versions: "to hide" (חָבָא), "to bury" (טָמַן), "to cover" (סָתַר), or "to camouflage" (צָפַן). The Greek family also includes the noun "hiding place" and compounds like "to hide before" or "to hide around." The basic image is that of secrecy, of the veiled, of what escapes observation.
G2928.emploi: This verb appears about 17 times in the New Testament, concentrated mainly in Matthew and John. It first describes the concrete action of concealing something (Matthew 25:18, 25) or withdrawing to flee (John 8:59). Very often it takes a figurative and theological meaning: the mysteries of the kingdom are hidden in parables (Matthew 13:35), divine wisdom is hidden from the proud (Matthew 11:25), the Christian's life is hidden with Christ in God (Colossians 3:3). In the passive voice, the word also emphasizes the disciples' inability to understand the Lord's secret words (Luke 18:34) or the secret of the truly faithful disciple (John 19:38). In Revelation, men seek to hide from the judgment of God (Revelation 6:15, 16).
G2928.portee: This word reveals the biblical opposition between what is manifest and what is hidden: what men see is not all, and the true reality—the presence of God, the reign of the Father, life in Christ—often escapes observation. For the Christian reader, to hide also reminds that the disciple should not fear to keep their convictions secret when threats loom (like Joseph of Arimathea), and that what is hidden will ultimately be revealed on the day of judgment. It is an invitation not to place one's identity or faith in shameful secrecy, but in God alone.

sens: To have the transparency and brilliance of crystal
To radiate with a luminous and translucent purity
To be of perfect and flawless clarity
G2929.detail: 1. The verb literally describes the brilliance of crystal: a substance that allows light to pass through while being perfectly transparent and smooth. It is the image of mineral beauty, a purity that sparkles. In Revelation 21:11, the light of the heavenly Jerusalem shines "like transparent crystal": it hides nothing, it reveals everything in absolute clarity. 2. Figuratively, it signifies clarity without mixture, a purity that reflects and amplifies light. It is the opposite of what is murky, opaque, or tarnished. This transparency suggests the absence of defect, stain, or obscure mystery. 3. The expression finally evokes an eternal beauty, that of the divine glory manifested: what shines like crystal fascinates with its perfection and fills with wonder those who behold it.
G2929.origine: The word comes from the Greek krystallos, "crystal," which designates a transparent and brilliant precious stone, a symbol of purity and perfection in antiquity. The verb is formed by the suffix -izō, which creates verbs from nouns ("to become like crystal, to shine like crystal"). The Greek λεγόμενον ("it is the only attested use") emphasizes the uniqueness and solemnity of this term in Revelation: John chooses this rare verb to express the transcendence of the heavenly city.
G2929.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Revelation 21:11. It is a hapax, meaning a word used only once. John uses it to describe the brilliance of the new Jerusalem in his final vision: not an ordinary light, but a light of absolute transparency and purity, that of jasper and crystal. This rare and precise vocabulary choice indicates that John seeks to express something inexpressible: the perfection and glory of God's eternal city.
G2929.portee: For the believer, this verb invites contemplation of the perfection that God prepares for those who follow him. The heavenly Jerusalem that shines like crystal symbolizes the glorious presence of God made visible, without veil, without trouble, without shadow. It is a promise that eternal life will have no shameful secrets, no relational opacity: everything there will be transparent, pure, luminous. This encourages those who go through earthly trials to set their gaze on this inaccessible yet certain splendor.

sens: Transparent and hard mineral substance, formed from ice or glass
Brilliance and crystalline purity, absence of disturbance or scintillation
G2930.detail:
1. Crystal is a brilliant and transparent mineral substance, as hard as ice. This is what John sees in his vision: a sea of glass like crystal before the throne of God (Revelation 4:6), a smooth and luminous surface that reflects divine holiness.

2. Crystal also evokes absolute purity and clarity. The river of the water of life that John contemplates flows from the throne of God, remaining as transparent and pure as crystal (Revelation 22:1), without any stain or opacity. The image suggests perfect clarity, the absence of anything that could disturb or tarnish.
G2930.origine: The Greek word κρύσταλλος comes from κρύος (cold, frost), as crystalline ice was understood in ancient times as extremely compact and brilliant frozen water. The word was then applied to any transparent and hard mineral substance resembling ice. In Hebrew, the word קֶרַח (ice) also refers to crystal in the Greek Old Testament.
G2930.emploi: This word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in the book of Revelation. John uses it to describe heavenly realities in his vision of heaven. First, the sea of glass before the throne shines like crystal, symbolizing the stability and purity of God's reign (Revelation 4:6). Then, the river of eternal life flows with crystalline clarity, without any impurity (Revelation 22:1). In both cases, the word reinforces the idea of radiant perfection and absolute transparency.
G2930.portee: The crystal in John's vision reminds the Christian that heaven is a place of purity and absolute clarity, without stain or darkness. It is an invitation to contemplate the beauty and holiness of God's throne and to aspire to this transparency and purity in one's own life with the Lord.

sens: In a hidden manner, away from sight
Out of the public eye, discreetly
In a concealed way, without witness
G2931.detail:
1. The adverb describes an action that takes place out of the sight of others, in secret. It is the opposite of what is visible or public. In Ephesians 5:12, Paul speaks of shameful acts that some do in secret: he refers to behaviors that one would never do in public because they would be ashamed.
2. The word emphasizes the idea of concealment: one acts "in secret" because one does not want it to be known, whether out of fear, shame, or malicious intent. This notion of hiding one's action recurs in all uses of the word.
3. Used in a spiritual or moral sense, "in secret" can also qualify an action done without a witness, including before God: it is a neutral adverb that simply describes the absence of an audience, before taking on a pejorative or laudatory nuance depending on the context.
G2931.origine: The word comes from a form of adverb in Greek constructed from a root meaning "to hide" or "to veil." This etymology underlies the entire family of words that express the idea of secret or hidden in Greek. The Greek Old Testament uses this term to render the Hebrew סָתַר (satar), which literally means "to hide" or "to veil," emphasizing what is removed from sight.
G2931.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Ephesians 5:12. Paul questions whether it is even proper to mention the degrading acts that some do in secret (that is, the hidden or unconfessed sins of those who claim to follow Christ). The context shows that Paul targets actions contrary to Christian ethics, done away from sight to avoid judgment or condemnation. It is a call to transparency and integrity: what is done in secret should not be done at all.
G2931.portee: This word invites the Christian to reflect on the integrity of their life: there is nothing we do in secret that God does not see. Jesus teaches that our secret acts will be revealed, and Paul reminds us that some acts are so contrary to Christian purity that it is even embarrassing to name them. This calls us to live in the light, without deceit, knowing that everything will be laid bare before God.

sens: Obtain something for oneself, procure
Become the owner of property or wealth
Gain or gradually constitute
Possess, hold as one's own
Conserve, keep for oneself (figurative sense)
G2932.detail:
1. To acquire is primarily to obtain something for oneself, to procure it by any means. It is the action of taking possession of what was not one's own: in Acts 1:18, Judas acquired a field with the wages of his crime — he bought it, he became its owner.

2. The word also refers to the wealth or goods one accumulates: when one "acquires the right of citizenship" in Acts 22:28, one gains a status or privilege through money or birth.

3. In the sense of gaining or constituting progressively, to acquire applies to what one builds over time. In Luke 21:19, Christ says that "by your perseverance you will save your souls" — to acquire here means to secure, to keep one's own life safe.

4. To possess is the stable result of having acquired: it is what one holds as one's own. In 1 Thessalonians 4:4, each must "possess his own body in holiness" — to master it as a possession one has in hand.

5. In a figurative and moral sense, to acquire can also mean to conserve, to keep for oneself what truly matters — one's dignity, integrity, eternal life.
G2932.origine: The Greek verb κτάομαι comes from a root expressing the idea of possessing and mastering. In ancient Hebrew, the verb קָנָה (qanah) conveys the same idea: to acquire, to buy, to constitute property. This root translates the fundamental act of man in the material realm: to procure what one needs, to build one's heritage. The word implies a voluntary action and duration: one does not acquire instantaneously; one obtains through effort, negotiation, or purchase.
G2932.emploi: The verb acquire appears 7 times in the New Testament, spread across Luke, Acts, and 1 Thessalonians. It primarily describes material purchase or ownership: Judas acquires a field, a tribune acquires Roman citizenship, Judas believed one could acquire God's gift for money. But the word also takes on a spiritual and ethical sense: to save, acquire, or keep one's soul through perseverance (Luke 21:19), to possess and master one's body in holiness (1 Thessalonians 4:4). The translations vary according to context (acquired, saved, price, body) but the fundamental meaning remains constant: to obtain and hold what one did not have.
G2932.portee: For the Christian, this word poses a crucial question: what are we truly acquiring? The New Testament uses it to denounce the illusion of believing one can procure God's gift through money, and to affirm that what matters is to acquire and keep eternal life through perseverance, as well as self-mastery in moral integrity. To acquire has value only if one acquires what endures.

sens: Possession that one holds, real or personal property
Wealth, accumulated fortune
What belongs to someone personally
G2933.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a concrete possession, a good that one owns — land, house, money. In the story of the rich young man (Matthew 19:22, Mark 10:22), he "had great possessions," meaning significant material wealth that he owned personally.
2. The word can emphasize the accumulated wealth and its weight in a person's life. It was because he was rich that the young man went away sad, refusing to abandon everything to follow Jesus: his possessions held him back.
3. In the context of the Jerusalem community (Acts 2:45, 5:1), the word refers to the properties that believers sold to share among themselves: what belongs to each one, their own heritage.
G2933.origine: The word κτῆμα comes from the verb κτάομαι ("to acquire," "to possess"), which expresses the action of procuring something to make it one's possession. The noun κτῆμα thus designates the result of this acquisition: what one has acquired and possesses. It is a term from the common vocabulary of Greek law and economics.
G2933.emploi: The word appears four times in the New Testament, always in a context of material wealth. Twice in Matthew and Mark to describe the "great possessions" of the rich young man, highlighting the importance of his fortune and the obstacle that his riches constitute to his discipleship. Twice in Acts to designate the properties that the early believers sold: first in the collective sense of community sharing in Acts 2:45, then more specifically in Acts 5:1 for the property that Ananias sold. In all cases, it refers to concrete possessions of value.
G2933.portee: This word challenges the reader regarding the role of material wealth in faith.
