The Gospel does not condemn possession itself but invites one not to be so attached to it that it becomes an obstacle to the relationship with God (Matthew 19:22). Acts, on the other hand, presents the giving of one's goods as an expression of brotherly love and new life in Christ: accumulation gives way to sharing.

sens: Beast of burden or transport (donkey, horse, mule)
Domesticated quadruped in general
Animal creature in a classification of living beings
G2934.detail:
1. The primary meaning of the word, and the most common in biblical usage, is that of an animal intended for transport or work: the Samaritan in the parable puts the injured man on his own mount to take him to the inn (Luke 10:34), and mounts are dispatched for Paul to be safely brought to the governor (Acts 23:24). It is a useful animal, owned and controlled by man.
2. More broadly, the word designates any domesticated quadruped, as opposed to other living creatures. Paul uses it in 1 Corinthians 15:39 to distinguish between different kinds of flesh: that of humans, that of quadrupeds, that of birds, and that of fish. The word groups all four-legged animals into one category.
3. In Revelation 18:13, among the goods of Babylon's trade are oxen and sheep — designated as full-fledged animals, exportable goods, and measurable wealth.
G2934.origine: The Greek word κτῆνος comes from κτάομαι (to acquire, to possess), as the animal was primarily a possession, a good. The Greek Old Testament translates the Hebrew בְּהֵמָה (beasts in a broad sense) and also מִקְנֶה (herds, owned livestock) with this word. The initial image is that of a good that one possesses, hence the particular nuance of domesticated or usable animal.
G2934.emploi: The word appears four times in the New Testament, always in practical or classificatory contexts. In the first three uses (Luke, Acts, 1 Corinthians), it clearly designates beasts of burden or useful domesticated animals. In Revelation, it appears among commercial riches. The word never applies to wild or marine animals: it remains limited to domesticated creatures or, broadly, to quadrupeds as a created category. Its usage is simple and direct, without particular moral or theological connotation.
G2934.portee: This word invites the reader to see domesticated animals as creatures that God entrusts to us and that we can use for our needs. The parable of the Good Samaritan shows a man who generously uses his mount to help an unfortunate person: it is one of the concrete acts of mercy. At the same time, the enumeration of creatures in 1 Corinthians 15 reminds us that the animal has its own place in God's creation, distinct from that of man.

sens: one who possesses, who has ownership of something
one who holds property, land
in a figurative sense, one who appropriates or controls something
G2935.detail:
1. The possessor is primarily one who holds ownership of something: a good, land, a house. The word simply describes the fact of having something personally, of legally possessing it. In Acts 4:34, the possessors of fields or houses were the landowners of Jerusalem, and they sold their properties to share the proceeds with those who had nothing.
2. More broadly, it refers to one who has and disposes of material goods. The word emphasizes less the wealth than the legal and concrete fact of being the owner of something — having something in one's personal power.
G2935.origine: The word comes from the verb κτάομαι (ktáomai), which means to acquire, to procure, to obtain in ownership. The possessor is one in whom the action of acquiring is completed: it is one who has acquired and holds. This root also appears in French in words like "ktèse" (acquisition in ancient Greek), reminding us that to possess is the fruit of an acquisition.
G2935.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 4:34. It describes the early Christians of Jerusalem after Pentecost: those who possessed lands or houses. Far from being pejorative, the word simply acknowledges the existence of property owners within the Church and highlights their gesture: they sell what they possess to meet the needs of the poor. It is thus a neutral term that serves to identify a social category in the context of brotherly sharing.
G2935.portee: This word reminds us that the early Church included people of means, and that faith in Jesus transformed the meaning they gave to their possessions: instead of keeping them jealously, they put them at the service of the community and the less fortunate. This shows that possessing goods is not an obstacle to generosity but can become an opportunity for sharing that testifies to the love of Christ.

sens: To make something exist that did not exist before
To produce, form, constitute
To establish, institute a new order or situation
To appoint someone to a position or state
To shape the soul or character of a person
G2936.detail:
1. The primary meaning is the action of bringing into existence from nothing: this is what God does in creating heaven and earth (Colossians 1:16: "for by him all things were created"). It is a divine and absolute act, reserved for God alone.
2. The verb can also mean "to produce" or "to bring forth": when God creates food (1 Timothy 4:3), he produces it for the use of men. It is an act of formation.
3. Create can mean "to establish" or "to institute": God creates in us a "new humanity" (Ephesians 2:15), meaning he establishes a new order or reality.
4. When speaking of a person, to create means "to transform" or "to reshape": we have been created "in Christ Jesus for good works" (Ephesians 2:10), which means that God forms and constitutes us in a new identity.
5. To create can apply to God as "Creator," the one who has absolute authority over all that exists (Romans 1:25: "the Creator").
G2936.origine: The verb κτίζω comes from a root meaning "to cut," "to shape." It is primarily a technical verb: it denotes the action of building or founding a city. In the Greek Old Testament, it mainly translates the Hebrew verb בָּרָא (to create), which expresses God's unique creative act. The Greek verb carries this nuance of a fundamental divine creation, distinct from mere fabrication.
G2936.emploi: The verb κτίζω appears about thirteen times in the New Testament, almost always referring to God's creative act. Matthew 19:4 and Romans 1:25 refer to God as the "Creator." Most uses concern the creation of all things: heaven, earth, visible and invisible beings (Colossians 1:16, Revelation 4:11). But the verb also applies to a spiritual or moral creation: God creates us in Christ Jesus to do good works (Ephesians 2:10), or he creates in us a new humanity (Ephesians 2:15, 4:24). Foods are also "created" to be consumed with thanksgiving (1 Timothy 4:3). The context shows that to create is to establish something lasting, whether it be the visible world or the transformation of the soul.
G2936.portee: This verb reminds us that God alone is the creator: everything that exists belongs to him and depends on him. For the Christian, knowing that he has been "created in Christ Jesus" means that his new life is not the result of his effort, but a gift from God. This is a reason for wonder towards the Creator and gratitude for what he gives us. It also establishes the honor due to God as the sovereign master of the universe.

sens: The act by which God created the world and all things
The entirety of created things, the world and all that populates it
Creatures as such, created beings
The order established by God, existing authorities and structures
A total renewal, a radical transformation
G2937.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the act of creation itself, the moment when God brought the universe out of nothing. Mark 10:6 uses it when speaking of the beginning: "But from the beginning of creation, God made them male and female." This act reveals God's power and divinity, as shown in Romans 1:20: "For since the creation of the world, his invisible attributes are clearly seen."
2. The word also refers to the entirety of creatures and the created world as a whole. Romans 8:39 speaks of a "creature" (any creature) that cannot separate us from the love of God. Colossians 1:15 affirms that Christ is "the firstborn over all creation," meaning he is above all that exists.
3. In particular, creation can refer to irrational creatures, that is, animals and nature. Romans 8:19-22 speaks extensively of creation subjected to futility and groaning in anticipation of deliverance.
4. The word can also mean the established order, the authorities and structures created by God. 1 Peter 2:13 urges submission to "every human authority" (literally "to every human creature"), meaning the established ordinances.
5. In 2 Corinthians 5:17 and Galatians 6:15, "new creation" refers to the radical transformation that Christ brings: anyone in Christ becomes a new creature, a new creation.
G2937.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb meaning "to found" or "to establish," and more broadly "to create." Originally, it denotes the act of founding a colony or a city. In the Bible, it has taken on the meaning of the creation of the world by God. This Greek word often translates the Hebrew word meaning "possession" or "acquired good," but also evokes the idea of something made, established, set in place durably. The word family includes the verb "to create" and the noun "creator."
G2937.emploi: The word appears 19 times in the New Testament, mainly in Paul and the Gospels. It is used in two main senses: on one hand, the act of creation and its beginnings (Mark 10:6, Mark 13:19, Romans 1:20), and on the other hand, the entirety of existing creatures (Romans 8:39, Colossians 1:15). Paul frequently uses it to affirm the relationship between God, Christ, and all that exists. The expression "new creation" in Paul refers to the transformation that God effects through Christ (2 Corinthians 5:17, Galatians 6:15). Romans 8:19-22 is a key passage where Paul personifies all of creation, showing it groaning and awaiting final redemption.
G2937.portee: This word reminds us that the world and all that exists depend entirely on God and his will. For the Christian, understanding that we are a "new creation" in Christ transforms the meaning of life: it is not a simple improvement of the old, but a radical break that remakes the whole being. Finally, seeing all of creation groaning and awaiting liberation gives the Christian a cosmic hope: God has promised to restore not only humanity but the entire universe.

sens: Everything that has been created, in contrast to the Creator
What exists by the will and action of God, from the greatest to the smallest
Living beings, animated or not
Everything formed by God in the universe
G2938.detail:
1. The word designates everything that exists because God created it — it is the work that comes from the hands of the Creator. It expresses the relationship of dependence between the creature and God: everything that is not God has been created by Him. In 1 Timothy 4:4, Paul states that "everything God created is good": each creature bears the mark of the goodness of its creator.
2. The creature can refer to each particular living being, such as the creatures of the sea in Revelation 8:9, "the third of the creatures that were in the sea and had life." These are beings endowed with their own life.
3. In Revelation 5:13, the word encompasses all creatures without exception: "All creatures that are in heaven, on the earth, under the earth, and in the sea" — a universal harmony of all that God has made, which together proclaim the glory of God and the Lamb.
4. In James 1:18, "the firstfruits of His creatures" refers to believers as the firstborn of the new creation that God began with the resurrection of Christ — a new creature in His intention.
G2938.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb κτίζω (ktízô), which means "to create, to found, to establish." The Greek borrowed this verb in the sense of a creation that did not exist before, notably the founding of a colony. In the Greek Old Testament, the same verb translates the Hebrew בָּרָא (bará), "to create," when God creates the heavens and the earth. The noun κτίσμα (ktísma) — "creature" — is thus the created being itself, the product of the creative act.
G2938.emploi: This word appears only four times in the New Testament, always in the Pauline epistles and Revelation. In 1 Timothy 4:4, Paul opposes those who forbade certain foods, affirming that every creature created by God is good. In James 1:18, the term refers to believers reborn according to God's will, forming the "firstfruits" of His new creation. In Revelation, this word broadens the vision to the entire universe: 5:13 describes all the creatures of the cosmos worshiping God together, while 8:9 speaks of the marine creatures that perish during the eschatological judgments. The word always expresses the notion of a being or reality that depends entirely on God for its existence.
G2938.portee: Understanding that we are creatures helps the Christian grasp their true status before God: we are not autonomous; we are purposefully created by the One who loves us. This establishes humility and gratitude. At the same time, the word elevates the dignity of creation: everything God created is good, and nothing should be despised. For the regenerated believer, being called a "creature" of God through spiritual resurrection expresses their new identity in Christ.

sens: one who creates, who brings something into existence
one who founds, who establishes
God as the author of creation
G2939.detail:
1. The creator is one who brings something into existence from nothing or who is its author: it is the act of creating. In classical Greek, this word was used to refer to a founder of a city or an institution.
2. In the Bible, this word specifically designates God as the one who created the universe and all things. The only occurrence in the New Testament is found in 1 Peter 4:19, where Peter invites Christians who are suffering to entrust their souls "to the faithful Creator": God, who created all things, is also faithful, meaning trustworthy and reliable in His promises.
3. The image is one of stability and solidity: the one who creates things holds them in hand and governs them.
G2939.origine: The word comes from the verb κτίζω (ktizô, to create), which literally means to bring into existence, to form, to establish. The root evokes the act of building or founding something durable. It is a word that is regularly used in the Greek translation of the Old Testament to translate the Hebrew verb "bara" (to create), notably in the creation account (Genesis 1). In classical and biblical Greek, it is a term of authority and absolute power.
G2939.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Peter 4:19. However, the family of the verb κτίζω (to create) is frequent, especially in Paul (Ephesians, Colossians) and in Revelation, always to speak of God's creative power. Peter uses it in a context of Christian suffering: it is precisely because God is the creator (the one who has absolute authority) AND faithful (the one who keeps His promises) that persecuted believers can confidently entrust their lives to Him. This choice of word emphasizes that God has not lost control of His creation, even in the worst circumstances.
G2939.portee: Calling God "the Creator" reminds the suffering Christian that their life belongs to the One who possesses absolute power and unwavering faithfulness. It is a word of encouragement: entrusting one's soul to the Creator is placing one's burdens in the hands of the One who governs all, who cannot lie, and who sees beyond present suffering. The title also affirms the dignity of each believer: one is not a forsaken creature, but loved by the very One who created us.

sens: Game of dice, throwing dice
Art of deceiving through tricks and stratagems
Way of seducing or perverting through false doctrines
G2940.detail:
1. The word literally comes from the game of dice (κύβος means die). Just as in dice one wins through trickery and chance, the word has come to designate deception and cunning in general.
2. It refers to the art of deceiving through stratagems, tricks: it is the ability to lead someone astray for personal gain. In Ephesians 4:14, Paul speaks of "the deception of men," meaning those cunning maneuvers by which false teachers seek to mislead Christians.
3. More specifically, it is the cunning employed to seduce minds: the context of Ephesians 4:14 shows that it involves false doctrines presented persuasively, designed to divert believers from the truth of the Gospel. It is an intellectual and spiritual trap.
G2940.origine: The word comes from the Greek κύβος (kubos), which means die or cube. In dice games, cheaters used tricks to win; hence, the word acquired the figurative meaning of cunning, deception, stratagem. It is a vivid image: the game of dice was associated with chance and deception, just like loaded dice or player manipulations.
G2940.emploi: The word κυβεία appears only once in the New Testament, in Ephesians 4:14. Paul uses it to qualify the cunning of false teachers who, through their deceptive eloquence and seductive doctrines, seek to divert Christians from the truth. The apostle contrasts this "deception" with spiritual maturity in Christ (verses 11-16): he wants the Church to grow in doctrinal stability and not be led astray by intellectual manipulations. The context shows that this deception is not a mere threat, but an active reality in the early Christian communities.
G2940.portee: This word warns us that faith requires spiritual vigilance and discernment. False doctrines never present themselves as such: they adorn themselves with persuasion and tricks to seduce. Knowing the Word of God and growing in spiritual maturity, as Paul urges, is to protect oneself against deception. For today's Christian, it is a call not to naively accept every religious interpretation, but to examine everything in the light of Scripture.

sens: Direction of a ship, piloting
Figurative sense: direction, administration of a community
G2941.detail:
1. In the literal sense, government (or piloting) is the art of directing a ship on the water, as an experienced captain would guide his boat through the waves. It is an image of mastery and guidance.
2. In the figurative sense, the word refers to the direction or administration of a community, particularly the Church. In 1 Corinthians 12:28, Paul lists the different gifts that God distributes to believers to build up the Church: after the apostles, prophets, and teachers, he mentions those who have "the gift of government," meaning the ability to wisely lead and guide communal life.
G2941.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb « kubernáô » (to govern, to direct), which literally means "to pilot" or "to steer a boat." This verb itself evokes the image of a helmsman (kubernétès) mastering the oars or the helm. The Hebrew word « tahboulah » (תַּחְבֻּלָה), translated by this Greek term in Proverbs, also means "counsel" or "wise direction." The central image remains that of guidance, of a course set with wisdom.
G2941.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Corinthians 12:28, where Paul describes the different charisms (spiritual gifts) that the Holy Spirit grants to the members of the Church. In this context, government is listed among the essential gifts for the life of the Christian community. It is a practical gift, useful for the administration and proper direction of the assembly, distinct from more spectacular gifts like miracles or healings.
G2941.portee: This word reminds us that leading a Christian community is not an ordinary human talent, but a gift of the Holy Spirit. It values those who wisely exercise the responsibility of leading the Church, a task as important for the common edifice as preaching or teaching. It is an invitation to recognize and honor the gift of spiritual leadership in the Church.

sens: one who directs a ship by guiding it
one who guides, who leads a people or a community
G2942.detail:
1. The pilot is the experienced sailor who holds the helm of a ship and guides it on the water, knowing the winds, currents, and hazards. In Acts 27:11, the centurion listens to the pilot of the ship rather than Paul, as he is trusted to navigate the boat safely. In Revelation 18:17, the pilots stand far off during the destruction of Babylon, losing their jobs and prestige.
2. In the figurative sense, this word refers to one who guides a community or a people, like a leader or governor overseeing those entrusted to him. The image of the expert pilot, who knows the way and masters the dangers, applies spiritually to any responsible leadership.
G2942.origine: The word comes from a Greek root denoting the action of governing and directing. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament (translated by this word in the ancient Greek version), we find the term « nocher » or « pilot » — one who holds the helm. This root evokes the idea of mastery, firm and wise direction.
G2942.emploi: The word κυβερνήτης appears only twice in the New Testament. In Acts 27:11, during Paul's journey to Rome, it refers to the pilot of the ship, a recognizable and respected authority figure. In Revelation 18:17, the pilots are among the horrified witnesses of Babylon's fall, an image of human vanity destroyed. The word remains linked to the direction of a ship or, by extension, to any exercise of authority and responsibility.
G2942.portee: This word reminds the believer that all direction — whether maritime, political, or spiritual — requires knowledge, experience, and wisdom. The pilot in Acts 27 embodies a human authority, certainly useful, but not to be placed above the word of God. And the image of the pilots fleeing Babylon invites reflection on the vanity of worldly powers.

sens: all around, on all sides
that encircles, surrounds
G2943.detail:
1. The word describes what is found or arranged on all sides of a person or thing. In Revelation 4:4, the apostle John sees "around the throne" twenty-four thrones where elders are seated: they completely surround him. It is a circular, spatial arrangement, very concrete.
2. It can also qualify what envelops, encircles something or someone. In verse 3 of the same chapter, the throne is "surrounded by a rainbow": the rainbow forms a crown all around the throne, protecting or magnifying it. The word emphasizes this enclosure, this presence that accompanies from all sides.
G2943.origine: The word comes from the Greek κύκλος (circle, cycle). It retains this idea of circular shape or movement around a central point. It is a locative adverb that places the action or object in a space completely surrounded. In Hebrew, it often translates סָבִיב (sabib), which has the same root meaning "to turn around."
G2943.emploi: The word appears only three times in biblical Greek, all in the vision of the heavenly throne in Revelation 4. John uses it to construct the image of heaven: first the throne surrounded by the rainbow (v. 3), then the thrones of the elders arranged in a circle around (v. 4), and finally the four living creatures filled with eyes "all around and within" (v. 8). This is not a trivial word: John uses it to give depth and harmony to his celestial description, emphasizing the concentric arrangement of things around God's throne.
G2943.portee: This word helps the reader visualize the heavenly liturgy: God at the center, heaven organized in concentric circles around Him, everything that exists revolves in an ordered harmony. It reminds us that God is at the heart of all things and that all creation surrounds Him in perpetual worship.

sens: To go around something while moving
To encircle something or someone with a barrier, fence, or army
To envelop someone or something in a way that isolates
G2944.detail:
1. The most concrete sense is that of going around an object, traversing its circumference: at Jericho, the Israelites went around the walls for seven days (Hebrews 11:30), walking around the city following its outline.

2. The word then denotes the action of encircling, enveloping a thing or a person with something that creates an obstacle or limit: Jerusalem is besieged by armies (Luke 21:20), meaning surrounded by soldiers who block it on all sides like a living barrier.

3. Finally, it expresses the idea of gathering around someone, encircling them to draw closer: the disciples surrounded Paul who had fallen to the ground (Acts 14:20), and the Jews gathered in a circle around Jesus (John 10:24) to question Him.
G2944.origine: The word comes from the Greek κύκλος (kuklos), which means "circle." The basic image is thus one of circular movement or arrangement in a round formation. In the Greek Old Testament, this verb often translates the Hebrew סָבַב (sabab), which has exactly the same meaning: to turn around something, to envelop it. The root κύκλ- is found in other French words like "cyclone" or "encyclopedia."
G2944.emploi: The verb κυκλόω appears four times in the New Testament. It first describes military encirclement: Jerusalem besieged by Roman armies (Luke 21:20, used in the passive; also recalled in Luke 19:43). It then applies to crowds or disciples gathering around a person: the Jews pressing Jesus with questions (John 10:24) and the disciples hurrying around Paul’s body (Acts 14:20). Finally, it describes a ritual act: the processional circuits around Jericho (Hebrews 11:30). In all cases, the emphasis is on the action of forming a circle or barrier, whether physical or human.
G2944.portee: This word reminds the reader that faith does not isolate: it unites believers around the Word and the Lord, just as the disciples gathered around Paul, or the Israelites united in obedience to God around Jericho. It also shows that external obstacles (a siege, a crowd) do not separate the believer from their trust in God. It is an invitation to remain together in faith, no matter what happens.

sens: Very close, in a space that surrounds something or someone
The lands, villages, or regions that are in the immediate vicinity
Around a central point, in all directions
G2945.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning: "around" describes what immediately surrounds someone or something. When Jesus looks "at those who were sitting around him" (Mark 3:34), he sees the people placed in a circle near him. This conveys the idea of immediate proximity, of people or things forming a perimeter.
2. The word is also used to refer to the surroundings of a place, that is, the nearby villages and countryside. When Jesus "went around the villages nearby" (Mark 6:6), or when it is said to the crowds that they can "go to the villages and the countryside nearby" (Mark 6:36, Luke 9:12), it refers to the territory immediately adjacent, accessible on foot.
3. In a broader sense, the word indicates a neighboring region: Paul "abundantly spread the Gospel" from Jerusalem "and the neighboring countries" to Illyricum (Romans 15:19), thus covering a whole geographical area around a starting point.
G2945.origine: The Greek word comes from κύκλος (cycle, circle, ring). The adverb κύκλῳ is the locative form (a case that expresses place), literally "in a circle" or "within a circle." This geometric origin recalls the initial image: that which forms a circle around a center. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, this word frequently translates סָבִיב (sabib), which carries the same idea of encirclement and proximity.
G2945.emploi: The word appears 8 times in the New Testament, mostly in the Gospels and Revelation. In the Gospels (Mark 3:34, 6:6, 6:36 and Luke 9:12), Jesus or his disciples use it to talk about what surrounds: the people sitting near him, or the nearby villages. Paul uses it once (Romans 15:19) to describe the geographical extension of his ministry, with the nuance of "neighboring countries." In Revelation (4:6, 5:11, 7:11), the word describes what surrounds the throne of God: the heavenly creatures placed around the throne. The meaning always oscillates between immediate proximity and the nearby environment, never far away.
G2945.portee: This word reminds us that in the Gospel accounts, Jesus is surrounded by his disciples and the crowd: he is not isolated, but at the heart of a community that surrounds him. This image of encirclement invites us to meditate on our place beside him. In Revelation, the creatures "around the throne" show us that all of creation converges towards God, in worship and permanent proximity. It is an invitation for us too to stand close to him.

sens: The act of rolling or tumbling in something
The state of one who abandons themselves to dirt or degradation
A habitual return to shameful or degrading practices
G2946.detail:
1. The word literally designates the action of rolling or wallowing in something — like an animal rolling in the mud. In 2 Peter 2:22, the washed pig wallows in the mire: after being cleaned, it returns to its natural state and rolls in the dirt.
2. More broadly, the word evokes the state of abandonment to degradation, the act of delighting in what is low or impure. It is the image of a creature that, instead of remaining clean, voluntarily throws itself into the mud.
3. By extension, wallowing expresses the obstinate and repeated return to shameful practices: the pig in the proverb does not wallow just once; it is its habitual behavior. This describes one who, after having left sin, deliberately returns to it and takes pleasure in it.
G2946.origine: The word comes from the verb κυλίω (kulio), which means to roll or to wallow. The form κύλισμα is a noun of action that literally designates the result or process of rolling. The image is that of an animal rolling in something — dust, mud, dirt. It is a concrete word that retains this animal image even in a figurative sense.
G2946.emploi: The word κύλισμα appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Peter 2:22. Peter quotes the proverb of the dog and the pig to describe false prophets and false teachers who have returned to their sinful practices. The image of wallowing expresses the deliberate and complacent return to sin after having known it — an even graver return because it shows that the person takes pleasure in it. It is a word chosen for its repugnant and concrete character: it paints the moral degradation of those who abandon the path of righteousness.
G2946.portee: This word reminds the believer that returning to sin after turning away from it is a form of voluntary abandonment of grace. The image of wallowing emphasizes how degrading this return is and contrary to the new life in Christ. For one who has tasted the freedom of forgiveness, returning to old practices is to freely choose dirt — a strong warning against complacency towards sin.

sens: To move by turning on oneself
To twist, to convulse on the ground
G2947.detail:
1. The verb describes the movement of something that rolls, that turns on itself to advance — like a stone pushed down a hill. This is the proper and physical sense of the word.
2. Applied to a person, it means to twist, to contort on the ground, generally as a sign of suffering or convulsion. In Mark 9:20, the possessed boy "rolled" on the ground foaming at the mouth: the verb shows the violence of the crisis, the body agitated and convulsing uncontrollably.
G2947.origine: The word κυλίω is a more recent form of the verb κυλίνδω, both expressing the idea of rolling or turning. In Hebrew, it often translates גָּלַל (galal), which has the same root as גַּל (gal), the "roll" or that which "rolls." This family of words evokes circular and uninterrupted movement, from the scroll of parchment to the stone rolling down a slope.
G2947.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Mark 9:20. It describes the behavior of the young epileptic (or possessed by an unclean spirit) when he sees Jesus: he falls to the ground and begins to roll, to twist violently, foaming at the mouth. This is a concrete detail that underscores the gravity of his condition and the power of the force that dominates him — a classic symptom of convulsions or possession according to the Gospel accounts.
G2947.portee: This word reminds us of the raw reality of suffering and spiritual oppression that Jesus came to combat. The detail of the body rolling, far from being picturesque, confronts us with the misery of one who does not have access to healing — until the coming of Jesus. It is a call to see in Jesus the liberator of those who suffer.

sens: deprived of the normal use of a limb, especially an arm or hand
mutilated, amputated
figuratively: rendered useless or ineffective
G2948.detail:
1. The word refers to a person struck by paralysis or physical infirmity affecting their limbs. In Matthew 15:30-31, Jesus heals a large crowd that includes "crippled" individuals alongside the lame, blind, and mute: these are people deprived of the proper functioning of their bodies, and their healing is a miracle that amazes the crowd.
2. More specifically, the word applies to someone who has lost or can no longer use a limb — an arm, a hand. This is the sense that Jesus uses in Matthew 18:8 and Mark 9:43: "it is better to enter life maimed" — that is, mutilated of a hand — than to be thrown into hell. It is not a real amputation that Jesus recommends, but a shocking image: renouncing what leads us to sin, even if it costs us dearly.
3. Figuratively, the word can evoke inefficiency or incapacity: a person or action that is "crippled" is hindered, rendered incomplete.
G2948.origine: The Greek word κυλλός comes from an ancient root that expresses the idea of bending, twisting, or folding. It carries the image of something that is deformed, bent, or twisted. In Hebrew, the Greek Old Testament often translates words describing lameness and physical infirmity with this term, particularly in the purity laws of the Temple (Leviticus) where certain infirmities excluded one from priestly service.
G2948.emploi: The word appears four times in the Gospels, only in Matthew and Mark, always in connection with healing or sacrifice. In the first two passages (Matthew 15:30-31), it literally refers to sick people whom Jesus heals, demonstrating His power and evoking the admiration of the crowd. In the other two passages (Matthew 18:8 and Mark 9:43), Jesus uses it figuratively: He employs the image of voluntary amputation (losing a hand) to express the extreme cost of turning away from sin. The power of the language lies in this striking comparison: it is better to sacrifice a limb than to lose one's soul.
G2948.portee: This word shows how Jesus heals infirmities that no one else can heal, revealing divine power. But beyond the physical miracle, it teaches us a crucial spiritual truth: there are realities more serious than bodily mutilation — eternal loss. Jesus invites us to take our struggle against sin seriously, even if it means making difficult sacrifices here on earth for eternal salvation.

sens: mass of moving water that rises and falls on itself
set of waves crashing against a ship
figurative use: chaotic and destructive force
G2949.detail:
1. The wave is a swell, this mass of water that bulges and rises to the surface of the sea before falling back. This is the most concrete image of the word: in Matthew 8:24, the disciples see the boat covered by the waves raised by the storm.
2. When the Bible speaks of waves in the plural (multiple successive waves), it often describes the repeated assault of waves against a boat. In Mark 4:37, the waves crash into the boat with such violence that it begins to fill with water; in Acts 27:41, it is the very violence of the waves that breaks the stern of the ship.
3. The word also takes on a figurative, spiritual meaning: the waves become the image of a chaotic and destructive force, hostile to the one who endures it. In Jude 1:13, the "raging waves" represent ungodly men who unleash themselves like uncontrolled waves, casting up "the foam of their impurities."
G2949.origine: The Greek word κῦμα comes from a root meaning "to swell" or "to be pregnant" (κύω), the image being that of a mass that expands and rises. It therefore naturally designates what swells: the water that swells at the surface of the sea. In the Greek Old Testament, it mainly translates the Hebrew word גַּל (gal), which has the same concrete meaning: a wave, a swell.
G2949.emploi: The word appears five times in the New Testament, always to describe the violence of the waters. Three occurrences concern the raging sea: Matthew 8:24 and 14:24, Mark 4:37 place these storm scenes at the heart of the narrative of Jesus' power over the elements. One occurrence describes a real shipwreck (Acts 27:41). The last occurrence, in Jude 1:13, moves from physical reality to use the wave as a metaphor for moral and spiritual chaos. The singular word "wave" dominates the Segond translation (three times), while "billow" appears twice to emphasize the idea of violent and repeated movement.
G2949.portee: These storm narratives teach that Jesus does not fear the violence of nature: He sleeps while the waves threaten. For the reader, the wave also becomes the image of everything that seems to engulf us — trials, temptations, the chaos of the world — and reminds us that the presence and authority of Christ dominate these seemingly uncontrollable forces. Jude's vision reverses the image: it warns that those who rebel against God are themselves swept away by waves of destruction, an image of the judgment that awaits ungodliness.

sens: percussion instrument made of metal, consisting of two discs that clash together to produce a bright sound
the metallic, loud, and hollow noise produced by this instrument
G2950.detail:
1. The cymbal is a musical instrument made of two metal discs (often bronze or copper) that produce a bright and resonant sound when struck against each other. It is a common instrument in Temple music and Israel's ceremonies to accompany songs and praises. Paul mentions it in 1 Corinthians 13:1 to evoke this brilliant sound.

2. Figuratively, the cymbal represents a loud but hollow noise, without true substance — a sound that resonates loudly but means nothing at its core. Paul uses it to say that, without love, even the most spectacular spiritual gifts (speaking in tongues, prophesying) become empty noise, a loud clamor devoid of living content.
G2950.origine: The word κύμβαλον (kumbalon) comes from κύμβη, which designates a cup or bowl-shaped container — an image that perfectly suits the two hollow discs of the cymbal. In Hebrew, this instrument is called מְצִלָּה (metsilah), and it is mentioned in the Psalms and the accounts of Temple worship, where it accompanies the praises of Israel. The Greek word thus captures the idea of a hollow, emptied object that resonates.
G2950.emploi: The word κύμβαλον appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Corinthians 13:1. Paul uses it in his great hymn to love to construct an image: one who possesses all spiritual gifts but lacks love is like "a sounding brass or a clanging cymbal" — that is, noise, nothing more. The real instrument, joyful in Temple worship, here becomes the symbol of what lacks essence, of what sounds hollow. Paul thus contrasts outward brilliance with the substance of the heart.
G2950.portee: This image brings us to the heart of Paul's message: what shines, what is visible, what makes noise is nothing without love. For the Christian reader, it is an invitation to seek depth rather than appearance, and to understand that all talents and spiritual powers remain barren if they are not animated by love for others.

sens: Aromatic spice derived from a small herbaceous plant
G2951.detail: 1. Cumin is a spice derived from the seeds of a herbaceous plant in the family Apiaceae. These small, elongated seeds have a warm and slightly bitter flavor, and have been a common and valuable seasoning in the East since ancient times. In Matthew 23:23, Jesus mentions cumin among the herbs that the Pharisees meticulously tithed — that is, gave a tenth as an offering to God — while neglecting the major commandments of the Law.
G2951.origine: The Greek *kuminon* comes directly from the Semitic *kammon* (Hebrew *kamôn*), attested in Isaiah 28:25 and 27. This same Hebrew word is translated by this Greek term in the Greek version of the Old Testament. Cumin was known in Mesopotamia and Egypt long before biblical times and remained an important commercial product during the New Testament period.
G2951.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Matthew 23:23. In this passage, Jesus addresses the scribes and Pharisees and criticizes them for their excessive concern for legal purity regarding small aromatic plants: they scrupulously paid tithes on mint, dill, and cumin, even on the herbs from their gardens. However, by focusing on these minor details of the Law, they neglected the fundamental principles — justice, mercy, and faithfulness. Cumin here embodies what is secondary compared to the true weight of the moral Law.
G2951.portee: Jesus uses cumin as an example of an external and nitpicky piety that forgets the essence of God's will. For today's reader, this word invites us to distinguish between religious formalism — obeying the letter of endless rules — and authentic obedience that encompasses justice, compassion, and loyalty to God. It is a reminder that our commitment to God must be based on love and truth, not on a bureaucratic zeal detached from the heart.

sens: A young dog or a small dog
Figuratively: a despised or excluded person
G2952.detail:
1. The word literally refers to a young dog or a small dog. In Matthew 15:27 and Mark 7:28, the Canaanite woman speaks of the little dogs that eat the crumbs falling from their masters' table: this is the concrete image of a domesticated animal tolerated in the house but occupying a lower place.
2. Jesus uses it figuratively to refer to non-Jews (Gentiles) who are excluded from the salvation offered first to the children of Israel (Matthew 15:26; Mark 7:27). This is not a cruel insult, but an image drawn from the table setting: just as the little dog receives the crumbs and not the whole bread, so the Gentiles do not have access to the promises made to the Jews. The Canaanite woman accepts this humble comparison and responds with faith, even turning the image to her advantage.
G2952.origine: The Greek word κυνάριον comes from κύων (kyon), meaning dog. The suffix -άριον is a diminutive that expresses smallness or affection towards the object. It is a common term for domesticated dogs in the house, as opposed to wild dogs or guard dogs.
G2952.emploi: The word appears only four times in the New Testament, always in the same account of the Canaanite woman (Matthew 15:26-27 and Mark 7:27-28), which is the healing of the Canaanite woman's daughter. Jesus uses it first to express the order of priorities: salvation must first reach the children of Israel. But the woman subtly and humbly turns this image around, recognizing that even the little dogs have a right to the crumbs. It is a moment where the humility and faith of a woman excluded from the chosen people provoke Jesus to extend His mercy beyond the borders of Israel.
G2952.portee: This passage teaches that humility and faith persist even in the face of apparent exclusion. The woman accepts the image of the little dog and transforms it into a plea of trust: she does not demand the whole bread, but simply asks for the crumbs. For the reader, this shows that the grace of Christ is not limited by borders or social status; it responds to sincere faith that perseveres with humility.

sens: Island in the eastern Mediterranean, located off the southwestern coast of Asia Minor
Native or originating inhabitants of this island
G2953.detail:
1. Cyprus is a large island in the eastern Mediterranean, southwest of present-day Asia Minor. It is an important land on the trade and religious routes of the ancient Mediterranean world. The apostle Barnabas was from there (Acts 4:36), and it hosted a thriving Christian community.
2. The word also refers to the inhabitants of the island, particularly those who participated in the first expansion of Christianity. Men from Cyprus and Cyrene came to Antioch to proclaim the Gospel to the Greeks (Acts 11:20), and Mnason, an early disciple from Cyprus, hosted the apostle Paul (Acts 21:16).
G2953.origine: The Greek name Κύπριος (Kuprios) simply denotes what belongs to the island of Cyprus, whose name in Greek is Κύπρος (Kupros). This island was famous in antiquity for its wealth in copper (the ancient Greek word for copper, kupros, might be related to the name of the island, although the etymology remains debated). The Greek term applies to the island itself and its inhabitants.
G2953.emploi: The word appears only three times in Acts, always in contexts related to the growth of the early Church. Barnabas, one of the pillars of the Jerusalem Church, is introduced as being from Cyprus (Acts 4:36). A few years later, believers from Cyprus are among those who bring the Gospel to Antioch, the Christian capital of the time (Acts 11:20). Finally, during Paul's journey to Jerusalem, a disciple named Mnason, a trustworthy man formerly established in Cyprus, receives him as a friend (Acts 21:16). These three occurrences show that Cyprus was an important center of early Christianity, with close ties to Jerusalem.
G2953.portee: Cyprus reminds us that the Gospel spread rapidly well beyond Jerusalem, reaching distant islands and cities. It also symbolizes how dispersed believers remained united by faith and brotherhood: Barnabas, although far from his homeland, played a central role in Jerusalem, and the believers from Cyprus actively participated in the mission to the Gentiles.

sens: Large island in the eastern Mediterranean, southeast of Asia Minor
G2954.detail: Cyprus is a large island located in the eastern Mediterranean, off the coasts of Syria and Asia Minor. It plays an important role in the missionary journeys of the early Christians. Barnabas, who was from there, accompanied Paul during his first missionary journey (Acts 13:4), and it was there that they separated when Mark caused a disagreement between them (Acts 15:39). Paul also passed near the island during his travels, such as when the ship taking him to Rome sailed along its coasts against contrary winds (Acts 27:4).
G2954.origine: The Greek name Kupros designates this well-known Mediterranean island in antiquity. Cyprus was famous in antiquity for its copper (the Latin word for copper, ‘cuprum’, derives from it), its cedar wood, and its commercial wealth. The island was a major trade crossroads between East and West.
G2954.emploi: Cyprus appears five times in the Acts of the Apostles, all mentions occurring at the heart of Paul's apostolic ministry. During the first great persecution in Jerusalem against the Church, scattered believers went to Cyprus to proclaim the Gospel (Acts 11:19). It is on the territory of this island that the first missionary journey of Paul and Barnabas began (Acts 13:4). Cyprus thus becomes one of the first places of Christian expansion outside of Judea, reaching both Jewish communities and, gradually, Gentiles. The references to the island illustrate the movements of the apostles and the vitality of the early Christian communities in the Mediterranean.
G2954.portee: Cyprus reminds the reader that the Gospel spread quickly and widely in the known world, far beyond Jerusalem. It symbolizes the first missionary expansion of believers, driven by the Holy Spirit and by courageous witnesses who turned their exile into an opportunity to serve. This island shows how persecution, instead of stopping the Church, scattered it and caused it to grow in new territories.

sens: To bend one's body or head downwards
To lower oneself to accomplish a task or action
To make a gesture of humility or submission
G2955.detail:
1. The verb primarily describes the physical action of bending one's body down, inclining the head or torso. When John the Baptist says he is not worthy to untie the strap of Jesus' sandals "by lowering myself," he precisely evokes this inclination of the body to perform a servile task (Mark 1:7).

2. The word also means to lower oneself to do something, to bend down in order to accomplish a particular action. Jesus lowered himself to the ground to write with his finger in the scene where he is confronted about the adulterous woman (John 8:6). This is a precise, intentional gesture motivated by purpose.

3. Finally, the act of lowering oneself often carries emotional or spiritual weight: it manifests humility, submission, or deference towards someone greater. The context with John the Baptist suggests an act of voluntary lowering, a recognition of unworthiness.
G2955.origine: The verb κύπτω comes from a root that evokes the action of bending or folding. In Hebrew, the Old Testament primarily uses the verb קָדַד (qādaḏ) to convey the idea of bowing the head, inclining the torso. It is a simple and vivid word, drawn from the observation of the human body bending.
G2955.emploi: The verb appears twice in the Gospels, at key moments where humility or compassion must be noted. In Mark, John the Baptist uses it to express his unworthiness: he cannot even lower himself to untie the sandals of the Messiah, a task reserved for a master’s most humble servant. In John, it is Jesus himself who lowers himself to write on the ground in front of the adulterous woman and her accusers, a gesture of tenderness mixed with discretion in the face of judgment. Both passages show the verb in action: it is not an abstract idea, but a movement of the body that speaks volumes about the soul.
G2955.portee: For the reader, these scenes of "lowering" reveal the inverted order of the Kingdom: the greatest (John the Baptist, then Jesus himself) accepts to lower himself. This physical posture becomes a sign of true spiritual greatness. It invites every Christian to see that humility is not weakness, but strength in the service of love.

sens: City in North Africa, capital of the ancient region of Cyrenaica (modern-day Libya)
Inhabitants or natives of Cyrene
Jews from Cyrene dispersed and settled elsewhere, notably in Jerusalem and Antioch
G2956.detail: Cyrene is a large Greek city founded in North Africa, in Cyrenaica. It was an important center of Judaism in the diaspora, with a significant Jewish community. Its inhabitants are called Cyrenians. In the Gospels, Simon of Cyrene is the passerby whom the Roman soldiers force to carry Jesus' cross (Matthew 27:32, Mark 15:21, Luke 23:26) — an ordinary man, likely Jewish, who came from his distant city for the festivals in Jerusalem. More broadly, Cyrenians appear as active witnesses of the new faith: some discuss with Stephen in Jerusalem (Acts 6:9), others proclaim Jesus to the Greeks in Antioch (Acts 11:20), and Lucius of Cyrene becomes a prophet and teacher in the Church of Antioch (Acts 13:1).
G2956.origine: Cyrene comes from the ancient Greek Κυρήνη (Kurēnē). The city was founded in the 7th century BC by Greek colonists from the island of Thera. It was famous for its wealth, particularly silphium, a valuable plant, and for its Greco-Hellenistic culture. Its importance had declined by the time of the New Testament, but it still maintained a strong Jewish presence and significant influence.
G2956.emploi: Cyrene is mentioned six times in the New Testament. The first three references (Matthew 27:32, Mark 15:21, Luke 23:26) concern Simon of Cyrene, presented each time as a man coming from the fields, conscripted to help Jesus carry his cross. The next three (Acts 6:9, 11:20, 13:1) show the Cyrenians as active and dispersed members of the early Christian community: Hellenized Jews who become witnesses of the resurrection and spiritual leaders of the nascent Church. This is an example of how the message of Jesus spread through travelers and migrants of the ancient world.
G2956.portee: Cyrene reminds us that salvation comes through ordinary people from afar. Simon of Cyrene, initially forced, physically carried Jesus' cross — a gesture that illustrates how everyone is invited to participate in the journey of faith. More broadly, the presence of Cyrenians among the first believers shows that the Gospel did not remain confined to Jerusalem: it spread to the nations through men and women from distant backgrounds, ready to proclaim it faithfully.

sens: Coastal city in Libya in North Africa
Center of African Judaism at the time
G2957.detail: Cyrene is a large port city in the region of Libya, in North Africa, founded by the Greeks. It became an important center of Jewish life, with a significant community of Jews established there for a long time. At Pentecost, in Jerusalem, there were residents of Cyrene who came to Jerusalem for the festival (Acts 2:10), which shows that the ties between the African diaspora and Jerusalem remained strong.
G2957.origine: The Greek name Kurēnē comes from the Greek city of Cyrene, established in North Africa. Its French spelling "Cyrène" follows the tradition of the Segond. The city was famous in antiquity as a major center of diaspora Judaism, with its own synagogues and schools of thought.
G2957.emploi: Cyrene is mentioned only once in the New Testament, in Acts 2:10, during the account of Pentecost. Luke lists the regions of origin of the pilgrims who came to Jerusalem to celebrate the festival: by naming Cyrene, he highlights the remarkable extension of the Jewish community to North Africa, showing how the Gospel addresses believers dispersed throughout the known world from its very beginnings.
G2957.portee: Cyrene reminds us that the message of Christ was not only directed to the Jews of Palestine, but to Jewish communities scattered throughout the Mediterranean world. The mention of this African city broadens the reader's horizon: from the very beginning of Acts, the Holy Spirit draws witnesses from afar to Jerusalem, foreshadowing the universal expansion of the Church.

sens: Roman governor of Syria
G2958.detail: Quirinius is the name of a Roman governor mentioned only once in the New Testament, in connection with the census ordered at the birth of Jesus. He is a historical figure attested in Roman records.
G2958.origine: Quirinius is the Greek form of the Latin name Quirinus or Quirinius. This Roman name comes from the root quiris, which referred to armed Roman citizens. The name was borne by important figures in the Roman Empire.
G2958.emploi: Quirinius appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 2:2, where he is presented as governor of Syria at the time of the census decreed by Emperor Augustus. It is in this context that Mary and Joseph go to Bethlehem for the census. This mention historically situates the event of the birth of Jesus.

sens: woman of high rank or free condition
woman who commands, mistress of the house
title of honor or address for a woman
G2959.detail:
1. The word "lady" refers to a woman of high social rank or free condition, as opposed to a servant or a woman of low status. She is a woman worthy of respect, established in a position of authority or dignity.
2. The "lady" is one who commands a household, who is its mistress: she directs the home and those who live there. It is the female equivalent of "lord" or "master."
3. The word is also used as a courteous title of address or respect towards a woman, similar to our use of the word "lady" or the English "lady." In 2 John 1:1 and 1:5, this woman is likely either a high-ranking Christian or a metaphor representing the Church itself.
G2959.origine: The Greek word "kuria" comes from the same root as "kyrios" (Lord, master), corresponding to the feminine form. The root evokes the authority and power of one who leads. In the Hebrew of the Greek Old Testament, this word translates notably "gheberet" (גְּבֶרֶת), which designates the wife of the master, the mistress of the house. This etymology shows that "lady" carries the idea of command and dignity.
G2959.emploi: The word "lady" appears twice in the New Testament, both in the second epistle of John (2 John 1:1 and 1:5). In these passages, John addresses "the chosen lady" and "the chosen lady." Commentators debate the identity of this lady: she may be a particular wealthy or influential Christian woman (which would justify the title of "lady"), or a symbolic figure representing the Church. The use of the title shows, in any case, the respect and dignity with which John addresses her.
G2959.portee: This word reminds the reader that women held places of honor and influence in the life of the early Church. John uses the term "lady" not to belittle, but to honor the one to whom he writes. For today's Christian, this illustrates that the Christian faith and church life concern everyone, and that women are recognized as worthy and responsible individuals.

sens: Belonging to the Lord, to Christ
Concerning Christ or emanating from his authority
Day dedicated to Christ and his resurrection
G2960.detail:
1. The adjective "of the Lord" indicates possession or belonging: something that belongs to Christ, that is His. In 1 Corinthians 11:20, Paul speaks of the "Lord's Supper" — the meal that Jesus instituted, which bears His name and reflects His authority.
2. More broadly, the word designates what emanates from Christ, what is under His authority or bears His mark. It is the adjective that establishes the idea of something "Christian" in the proper sense: that which pertains to Christ.
3. Applied to the day, "the day of the Lord" (Revelation 1:10) designates the day dedicated to Christ and his resurrection — Sunday, the first day of the week, which the early Church celebrates in His honor and in memory of His work.
G2960.origine: The adjective comes from the Greek word "Lord" (κύριος, kurios). In classical Greek and in inscriptions, it primarily means "of the master, of the owner." The adjective applies to anything that depends on an authority or a person — their goods, their decisions, their days. In the New Testament, it is naturally applied to Christ the risen Lord: the meal, the day, the words that come from Him or that belong to Him.
G2960.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament according to our sources. In 1 Corinthians 11:20, Paul uses it to refer to the meal instituted by the Lord at the Last Supper — what would later be called the Eucharist or the Lord's Supper. In Revelation 1:10, he qualifies the day of the Lord, that is, the first day of the week, Sunday, which John celebrates in vision and dedicates to the worship of the risen Lord. Both uses are liturgical: they describe acts and moments that belong to Christ and that order the life of the Church.
G2960.portee: This small adjective expresses a crucial truth for the Christian: certain days, certain gestures, certain meals bring us directly closer to the risen Lord. When we speak of the Lord's Supper or the day of the Lord, we are not talking about human conventions, but about the presence and authority of Christ. This reminds the believer that their church life — their worship, their times of communion — is entirely ordered by and towards the Lord.

sens: To exercise authority over someone or something, to be the master
To govern, reign, command
To impose oneself with force, to take control
Figuratively: to have power over, to extend over (sin, death, the law)
G2961.detail:
1. The primary and most concrete meaning is to exercise sovereign authority: to be the master, the one who commands and governs. In Luke 22:25, Jesus declares that the kings of the nations "dominate" over their people; this is the exercise of political and hierarchical power, establishing a clear superiority.
2. In 2 Corinthians 1:24, Paul refuses to "dominate" over the faith of the Corinthians: he does not want to impose his authority, but to contribute to their joy. It is the same verb applied to the pastoral relationship — to have power over someone.
3. The usage appears in Romans 6:9 (death no longer dominates Christ) and Romans 6:14 (sin will no longer dominate the believer), where what "dominates" is presented as a power that imposes itself and governs. Romans 7:1 speaks of the law that "exercises its power" as long as a person lives: a force that applies and governs.
4. In 1 Timothy 6:15, God is called the Lord of "lords" (literally: the one who dominates over all those who dominate), expressing absolute supremacy.
G2961.origine: The verb comes from κύριος (kurios), which means "master," "lord." It literally means "to be kurios of something," that is, "to be master," "to exercise mastery." In Hebrew and Aramaic of the Old Testament, this verb often corresponds to the word מָשַׁל (mashal), which means to reign, dominate, govern. The family of the Greek word includes κυριότης (sovereignty) and other derivatives that all revolve around the idea of lordship and sovereign power.
G2961.emploi: This verb is used 7 times in the New Testament, mostly in the Pauline epistles. It first describes ordinary political and hierarchical power (kings over their subjects in Luke 22:25). Paul then uses it in a major theological perspective: in Romans 6 and 7, he speaks of the spiritual powers that dominate — sin, death, the law — and how the believer is freed from their domination by Christ. This is a key to understanding justification and sanctification: the heart of Paul's message is that these powers no longer have authority over the Christian. Paul also refuses to use this pastoral power himself in 2 Corinthians 1:24, preferring edification over authoritarianism.
G2961.portee: This word reveals a foundational reality of the Christian faith: the believer is no longer under the domination of sin, death, or condemnation. It shows that freedom in Christ is not an absence of law, but a transition from an oppressive authority (that crushes us) to the authority of the risen Lord (who saves us). It is also a call to leaders: to command without dominating, to serve rather than reign, as Jesus teaches.

sens: One who has authority, who commands: master, boss
God the Father, the Lord of the Old Testament
Jesus Christ after His resurrection and exaltation
Term of respect towards a superior, a master, a magistrate
G2962G.detail:
1. The word primarily designates one who possesses authority and power over something or someone. It is the master of a house, the owner of a field, one who has servants under his command (Matthew 9:38: "Pray to the Lord of the harvest to send out workers"). The basic image is that of a person who directs, decides, and has the right to command.
2. In the Old Testament translated into Greek, this word most often translates the name of God, the Lord (יהוה). In the New Testament, it thus designates God the Father Himself: "the Lord of heaven and earth" (Matthew 11:25). It is the most common title used to refer to God in the Pauline and apostolic letters.
3. After the resurrection of Jesus, this same word becomes the confessional title of Christians to designate Jesus Christ: "Our Lord Jesus Christ." By calling Jesus "Lord," the disciples affirm that He now possesses, along with God the Father, supreme authority over all things (Galatians 6:14: "the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ").
4. The word is also used as a respectful address towards masters, teachers, magistrates, and persons of authority (Luke 9:57: a man said to Jesus, "Lord, I will follow you"). It is a way to show respect and acknowledge the position of the one being addressed.
G2962G.origine: The Greek word kurios comes from a root indicating power and authority (kyros). In classical Greek, it designates one who has the power of decision, the master of a house, the owner. In the Septuagint (Greek translation of the Old Testament), this word was chosen to translate the divine name "Lord" (יהוה), which has given the word a sacred and theological dimension. This translation has greatly influenced the New Testament, where kurios designates both God the Father and, after Easter, the exalted Christ.
G2962G.emploi: This word appears more than 600 times in the New Testament, making it one of the most important in Christian vocabulary. It is first used for any hierarchical superior: master, owner, magistrate (Acts 16:16). But very quickly, and especially, it becomes the almost exclusive title of God and Christ. In Matthew, Mark, and Luke, Jesus is called "Lord" by His disciples and by the sick who plead with Him. In Paul and in the epistles, the expression "Lord Jesus Christ" or "Lord Jesus" is almost formulaic, appearing in almost every letter. The usage shows the evolution of apostolic understanding: from Jesus as a beloved master to Jesus as the risen Lord, worthy of the same worship as God the Father (Romans 14:8: "Whether we live, we live for the Lord").
G2962G.portee: For the Christian, confessing Jesus as "Lord" (Romans 10:9) is the fundamental act of faith. This title expresses not only reverence or respect but affirms that Jesus Christ has received from the Father all power and authority, and that His will is imposed on our lives. The title "Lord" also reminds us that there is one Master above all others, and that our Christian freedom consists in serving Him alone. This is why this word permeates the entire life of prayer and trust of the believer.

sens: One who has authority over someone, who commands servants or slaves
One who teaches or directs
One who possesses or depends on something
Title of respect addressed to a person of authority
God, sovereign and creator of the universe
Jesus Christ, the risen Lord
G2962H.detail:
1. The master is primarily one who has power and authority over others, especially over servants or slaves. The servant is not greater than his master: it is a relationship of inequality where one commands and the other obeys (John 15:20). Jesus uses this image to explain what His disciples should expect from those who will persecute them.
2. It is also one who directs a group or property: the master of the house shuts the door (Luke 13:25), the master of the vineyard sends his workers to work (Luke 20:13). It is a position of responsibility and decision.
3. The word designates the person who is addressed with respect, especially in social or religious relationships. People call Jesus "Lord" recognizing Him as someone greater than themselves (John 4:11).
4. For believers, the Lord is God Himself, sovereign over all things, creator of heaven and earth (Matthew 11:25).
5. In the New Testament, Jesus Christ is proclaimed Lord after His resurrection: Christians acknowledge Him as having absolute authority and obey Him as they would God (Romans 14:8).
G2962H.origine: The word κύριος (kurios) comes from a root meaning "one who has power" or "one who has authority." In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates the divine name YHWH (which the Jews did not pronounce aloud), but also the Hebrew words that designate a master or lord. This choice of the Greek word to speak of God shows how the early Christians transferred the language of divine power to Jesus Christ after His resurrection.
G2962H.emploi: The word κύριος appears more than 80 times in the provided passages. It is first used in the ordinary sense to designate a master or a boss to whom one obeys: Matthew often uses this word in parables (Matthew 20:8, 25:24). Luke uses it extensively in contexts of domestic servitude (Luke 12:36-47, 14:21-23, 16:3-8). Then, it becomes a title of respect addressed to someone in authority, particularly to Jesus, who is often called "Lord" by those who seek His help or instruction (John 4:11, 4:49). Finally, in Paul and in the epistles, the title focuses on Jesus Christ as the risen Lord to whom the heart and life of the believer belong (Romans 14:4, 1 Corinthians 8:5, Colossians 3:22). The word thus carries a progression: from temporal master to eternal Lord.
G2962H.portee: For the Christian, using "Lord" to refer to Jesus is not mere politeness: it is the affirmation that the risen Jesus exercises authority over their entire life, comparable to that of God the Father. Recognizing Jesus as Lord means obeying Him and entrusting one's existence to Him, just as a servant depends on his master. This transforms the understanding of faith: it is not an optional choice among others, but total allegiance.

sens: Sovereign power, supreme authority exercised by one being over others
Dignity, high rank attached to a position of authority
(In the plural) Categories of spiritual or celestial beings endowed with authority
G2963.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the power to exercise authority, the right to command. It is authority in itself, considered as a capacity to govern. In Ephesians 1:21, Christ is placed "above all dominion, authority, and power": these different words enumerate the forms of power recognized in the created universe.
2. The word can also signify the dignity or rank that accompanies power. It is less about the power exercised than the status, the honor one is entitled to by virtue of governing. In Colossians 1:16, the "dignities" are listed among created realities, alongside "thrones" and "dominions".
3. When used in the plural, it denotes beings or powers: the "dignities" then become spiritual creatures invested with their own authority. This is the case in almost all occurrences in the New Testament, where this term appears in enumerations of celestial hierarchies.
G2963.origine: The word comes from "kyrios" (Lord, master), which designates one who has authority. A dominion (kuriotès) is therefore what belongs to the Lord, what pertains to His nature as master. The verb from the same family means "to exercise power" or "to be lord of". It is a substantivized form that captures the idea of the state or function of one who dominates.
G2963.emploi: The word appears four times in the New Testament, always in the singular or plural in contexts of spiritual and celestial authority. In Ephesians 1:21, Paul lists the various forms of power to affirm the supremacy of the risen Christ. In Colossians 1:16, the "dignities" are mentioned as created beings in Christ and by Christ, suggesting that no power escapes His lordship. In 2 Peter 2:10 and Jude 1:8, the same word designates the powers that false teachers and the ungodly despise or insult: there is a refusal to recognize legitimate authorities, whether celestial or earthly. The context of crisis and divine judgment emphasizes that despising the "authorities" is a sign of rebellion against the order established by God.
G2963.portee: This word teaches the believer that all power and authority — in heaven, on earth, and under the earth — come from God and remain subject to Him in Jesus Christ. It invites respect for legitimate authorities, as they participate in the created order. At the same time, it warns against those who reject the authority of God and His institutions: this rebellion will have serious consequences, and it reveals a heart attached to the flesh rather than to God.

sens: To make a decision, agreement, or testament valid and official
To give approval or assent to something
To guarantee the legal or moral validity of an act
G2964.detail:
1. This verb primarily means to officially validate a commitment or act. For example, in Galatians 3:15, Paul speaks of a human testament that "is in good form": he means that once validated, no one can annul or modify it. It is like affixing an official seal to a document.
2. The word can also express active approval, the assent one gives to someone. In 2 Corinthians 2:8, Paul urges the Corinthians to "show love" to a man in difficulty: confirming their love in this way is to manifest it publicly and definitively.
3. More broadly, κυρόω means to confer authority and binding force to something — to make it obligatory, to put it into effect. It is the act by which a promise or law becomes enforceable.
G2964.origine: The verb comes from the noun κῦρος, which means "authority" or "power" — and also "validity" or "legal force". The basic idea is that of the authority that makes something official and binding. It is a word from the Greek world of business, contracts, and administration, where legitimate authority was necessary to seal an agreement.
G2964.emploi: κυρόω appears only twice in the New Testament. In 2 Corinthians 2:8, Paul uses it to call the Corinthians to put their love into action — the verb in the sense of "to accomplish" or "to publicly manifest". In Galatians 3:15, he uses it in the passive voice to speak of a testament "validated" or "in effect": once a legal act is established according to the rules, no one can revise it. In both cases, it is about an enforcement or validation that genuinely engages.
G2964.portee: This word reminds us that Christian promises and commitments are not empty: when we affirm our faith or love, it is a word that must materialize and remain firm. Just as a validated testament cannot be revoked, so our commitment to God, once affirmed, must hold. This gives weight to our spiritual decisions: to confirm something in Christ is to make it definitive and binding for our lives.

sens: Domestic animal known for its loyalty and attachment to humans
Impure or despicable creature, in biblical imagery
Corrupted, perverse, or hostile person to the Christian faith
Eater of scraps, being reduced to begging
G2965.detail:
1. The dog is primarily the ordinary domestic animal, a companion to humans. In the parable of the rich man and Lazarus, dogs lick the sores of the rejected beggar (Luke 16:21): even the beasts show more compassion than the indifferent rich man.
2. In the Mosaic law, the dog was considered impure. The Bible uses this word to stigmatize what is abject or repugnant, what defiles. When the psalmist says, "the dog returns to what it has vomited" (2 Peter 2:22), he depicts the return of the sinner to his past filth: the image of the animal becoming impure again after a temporary cleansing.
3. In the apostolic letters, "dog" becomes an insult hurled at the enemies of the Gospel. Paul warns: "Beware of dogs" (Philippians 3:2), meaning the false teachers who tear apart the Church like wild dogs. At the end of times, Jesus excludes from Heaven "dogs", meaning those who remain willfully enemies of God (Revelation 22:15).
4. The dog that feeds on crumbs fallen from the table evokes baseness, hunger, the state of one left at the door: it is the condition of the poor, the outcast, the one who survives on the leftovers of others.
G2965.origine: The Greek word κύων (kuōn) comes from an ancient root and is found in Latin canis, Hebrew כֶּלֶב (keleb), and our modern languages (dog, chien, Hund). In biblical Hebrew, keleb was also a term of insult. The Greek word regularly translated this Hebrew term in the ancient Greek Bible. The root evokes the barking or cry of the animal; it carries with it the image of the faithful beast, but also of the impure creature according to Jewish thought.
G2965.emploi: The word "dog" appears 5 times in the New Testament, always in the context or image of the animal itself or its rejection. In the Gospel of Luke, it retains its concrete meaning: the street dog licking the wounds (Luke 16:21). In other occurrences — Matthew, Philippians, 2 Peter, Revelation — the term shifts to the figurative. It becomes a label of insult: Jesus uses it to forbid His disciples from wasting the Gospel on those who would trample it (Matthew 7:6), Paul uses it to describe the false apostles who cause harm (Philippians 3:2), and the text of the Final Judgment reserves it for the eternally excluded (Revelation 22:15). Between the real dog and the dog insult, the Bible plays on the impurity and contempt attached to this beast.
G2965.portee: Understanding that "dog" in the Bible is never neutral: it is a word that wounds and excludes. For the Christian reader, it first reminds us of Jesus' love for the despised Lazarus, who even receives the visit of street dogs. But it also warns: the Word of God is not to be thrown before anyone, and those who willfully reject it, who tear apart the Church, who return to sin are linked to this image of baseness and rupture.

sens: The dead body of a person
The mortal remains of a human being
What remains of a dead person as inert matter
G2966.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a member of the body, a living and animated part — the original sense. But it comes to designate the whole body after death: a corpse, what remains when life has departed. In Hebrews 3:17, it refers to the corpses of the Israelites who perished in the desert for forty years, whose bodies fell to the ground without being able to enter the Promised Land — an image of God's judgment against those who refuse to trust Him.
2. The word is used to speak of the physical body devoid of life, emphasizing its material and mortal aspect. It is a stark reality: death returns man to the state of inert matter.
G2966.origine: The Greek word κῶλον comes from a root meaning "to cut" or "to divide." Originally, it designated a member, a part of the body — what can be cut or separated. The Greek Bible (the Septuagint) uses it to translate the Hebrew פֶּגֶר (peggèr), which means corpse or carcass, particularly for the remains of God's enemies or rebels. The meaning has thus evolved: from "separated member" to "body separated from life," that is, corpse.
G2966.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 3:17. The author cites it by referencing a passage from the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament) to remind of the punishment inflicted by God on the Israelites in the desert who doubted Him. The usage is grave and solemn: it marks the irreversibility of divine judgment. This word is not common in the Greek New Testament; the evangelists prefer other terms to speak of the dead or corpses. Its use here underscores the authority and weight of the ancient Scripture in the warning addressed to the Hebrews.
G2966.portee: This word reminds us of a dark but essential truth: the refusal of faith in God leads to death and judgment. The corpses fallen in the desert are not merely a historical detail, but a warning for every believer. The author to the Hebrews invites his readers to learn the lesson: do not fall into unbelief like those ancestors, for it leads to death. It is a call to vigilance and trust in God.

sens: To stop someone or something in its action or movement
To prohibit or refuse to allow
To oppose an action, a will
To restrain someone from doing something
G2967.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: to prevent someone from going somewhere or doing something by blocking or stopping them. Jesus reproaches His disciples for preventing little children from coming to Him (Matthew 19:14): they were physically stopping or pushing them away.

2. It also means to prohibit or refuse; to say "no" to someone. Jesus' accusers claimed that He "prevented" paying tribute to Caesar (Luke 23:2), meaning He defended or prohibited it.

3. The word means to oppose a will or a plan: when Peter wants to prevent someone from speaking in tongues, Jesus tells him not to oppose those who are not against them (Luke 9:50).

4. Finally, it means to restrain someone from performing an act: the centurion "prevented" his soldiers from executing Paul (Acts 27:43), restraining them from killing him.
G2967.origine: The word comes from a root that evokes the idea of blocking or barring the way. In Hebrew, it often translates verbs like כָּלָא (kālā, "to restrain") and מָנַע (mānáʿ, "to prevent"). The family of the Greek word includes the compound διακωλύω ("to strictly prohibit"), which reinforces the idea of obstacle or barrier.
